After the research, a fixed rule using only 2022-2023 results selects a low-correlated factor pool from all candidates the model produced, and scores it on unseen 2024-2025 data after removing common style returns such as size and momentum; the same rule on round-0 candidates alone gives a report baseline that "implements the report without iterating". We run gpt-6.1-sol (reasoning effort xhigh), gpt-6.1-terra (xhigh), muse-spark-1.3 (xhigh) and deepseek-v4.1-flash (max) once on each of 7 reports. Of the 28 runs, 19 factor pools pass the usability threshold; the average score is 48.4 (0-100 scale), against 25.4 for the report baseline and 35.9 for the models' own picks. From similar report baselines (17.0-31.0), the models separate after iteration to 74.7 (gpt-6.1-sol), 56.6 (gpt-6.1-terra), 35.8 (deepseek-v4.1-flash) and 26.2 (muse-spark-1.3); their candidates look equally good in training and diverge only in testing, with the leaders proposing more diverse ideas per round and ending with more effective factors in the pool. Evaluating research agents thus requires scoring on frozen future data after removing styles, and measuring "what the research produced" separately from "what was finally picked".

items.title: Instant-LIVO: Efficient LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry with Compact Geometry and a Bounded Single-Reference-Frame Map
items.summary: LiDAR-Inertial-Visual Odometry (LIVO) is a fundamental technology for autonomous systems; however, deployment on resource-constrained platforms remains challenging due to physical limitations. This paper presents Instant-LIVO, a tightly coupled, high-speed, real-time LIVO system. The system introduces a compact geometric map based on spatial-hashed OctVox and accelerates local-neighborhood retrieval and plane fitting through cache-assisted heuristic staged K-nearest-neighbor searches. It also employs a bounded single-reference-frame visual map that adaptively updates the reference frame according to the tracking status, while using Schmidt-type uncertainty-aware photometric fusion to maintain the correlation between the reference pose and the current state. The system performs multisensor fusion through a sequential process consisting of IMU prediction, LiDAR geometric correction, and visual photometric correction. It was evaluated on 32 public benchmarks and custom datasets. While maintaining competitive accuracy on both X86 and ARM platforms, Instant-LIVO achieves average processing-speed improvements of approximately 2.3x and 2.1x, respectively, and reduces peak memory usage to approximately 1/20 and 1/13, respectively. The results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing LIO and LIVO baselines in both accuracy and computational efficiency.The implementation is available at: https://github.com/Faker-0714/Instant-LIVO.git.

items.title: Learning Inside Types: Epistemic Typestates for Safe Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Type disciplines make programs safe by construction: components checked against each other's types compose into programs that cannot go wrong in the ways the types exclude. Types suit reinforcement learning: a type constrains what an agent may choose, not how it chooses, so the guarantee holds for every policy a learner produces. We introduce epistemic typestates, a type discipline for safe multi-agent reinforcement learning. An agent's type is a protocol whose states record its beliefs, the worlds it cannot rule out from its own observations and actions, and permits only actions that are safe in every world of the belief, whatever the others do within their public types. Agents learn inside their types, which are built and checked one agent at a time and run without communication. We prove type soundness and team safety, give a synthesis that is sound and complete, build types from guards when worlds are infinite, and show that shields are a special case. All proofs are mechanised in Rocq. On nine benchmarks, no typed learner causes a safety violation, and task performance does not differ significantly from that of two recent multi-agent shielding methods. Where a contract-based method fails at five and ten agents, types for ten agents are built in under a second. In the two continuous benchmarks, Lagrangian learners cause thousands of violations in every training run.

items.title: Segment Everything, Materialize Nothing: Exact Streaming Inference for Many-Class 3D Segmentation
items.summary: Whole-body segmentation tools such as TotalSegmentator and MOOSE split more than 100 classes across five or six networks. The reason is memory. Standard 3D inference, as implemented in nnU-Net and MONAI, holds a logit for every class and voxel, on the working grid and again on the scanner's grid. For a median whole-body CT at 125 classes, that is 76 GB. We show that this memory wall lies in what inference materializes, not in the task, and remove it without approximation. Every step after the network is local along one axis, so its outputs can be streamed through a ring one patch thick. The classification head commutes with blending and resampling, so the ring carries the network's features instead of the class logits. Memory thus no longer grows with classes times volume, and the label map on the scanner's grid stays exact. This holds for any model with a pointwise affine head, without retraining. Many-class models, previously impractical, become deployable. One model trained on all classes matches or slightly exceeds the toolkits' five or six specialists in segmentation quality and runs 5.8-15x faster end to end, with 3.2-7.6x less RAM and under 8 GB of VRAM. We provide the method as a drop-in for nnU-Net, TotalSegmentator and MOOSE. The code is part of nnU-Net (https://github.com/MIC-DKFZ/nnUNet), and unified models for both toolkits will be released.

items.title: WAM-Sim0.1: World Anchored Memory Meets Online RL for Consistent and Realistic Driving Simulation
items.summary: Autoregressive driving world models systematically suffer from structural drift, identity drift, and quality decay over long rollout horizons due to transient conditioning signals that lack persistent state. We present WAM-Sim, a driving world model anchored by a persistent hierarchical memory and optimized via online flow-matching RL. WAM-Sim structures persistent context across three temporal and semantic scales: pose-aligned structural tokens encoding persistent road topology, read-only scene tokens supplying geolocated background appearance, and write-once instance tokens preserving individual traffic participant identities across occlusions and chunk boundaries. To restore visual sharpness and physical plausibility degraded by multi-scale conditioning, we introduce an online post-training framework that optimizes self-generated rollouts via flow-matching RL guided by hierarchy-aligned visual rewards and a vision-language model physical judge. The invariant memory empirically confines policy optimization within the anchored context, helping suppress semantic collapse and reward hacking, while online RL systematically enforces physical commonsense and fine-grained visual fidelity. On the nuScenes benchmark, WAM-Sim achieves a superior generation fidelity (FID=3.47, FVD=25.72) and strong downstream perception performance (24.16 mAP, 71.23 road mIoU). On minute-scale rollouts of self-collected data, WAM-Sim substantially mitigates structural and identity drift, preserving high scene similarity and subject identity coherence across extended horizons. Project page: https://fudan-generative-vision.github.io/WAM-Sim.

items.title: Does Learning Order Explain Forgetting? The Lie Bracket as an Early-Warning Signal for Catastrophic Forgetting Without Old Data
items.summary: A network trained on task A and then task B ends at different weights than one trained on B and then A. To leading order this gap is set by the Lie bracket of the two tasks' gradient fields, and Dherin (2023) conjectured that a non-vanishing bracket may be linked to catastrophic forgetting. I test this conjecture empirically. Across Split MNIST, Split Fashion-MNIST and Split CIFAR-10, the forgetting of A is almost exactly the difference in A's loss between the two training orders (Spearman rho = 0.96-1.00). I then ask whether the bracket can predict that forgetting early in training on B and without any of A's data, using only a small summary stored when A finishes: its gradient and its top 20 Hessian eigenpairs. When the old task is well learned and forgetting is slow (task-incremental), this stored bracket ranks forgetting with rho = 0.70-0.81, against 0.33-0.58 for the penalty of Elastic Weight Consolidation, and matches or exceeds re-evaluating A on its own data. When forgetting is fast (domain-incremental), the stored summary goes stale and the EWC penalty is as good or better. The bracket fails outright when the old task is only half learned; I trace this to a residual gradient on A an order of magnitude larger, which makes first-order (slope) damage matter. In five-task sequences with slow forgetting, the stored bracket outperforms the EWC penalty on MNIST and CIFAR-10 features (by 0.16-0.17) and ties it on Fashion-MNIST; it fades as summaries age on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, where a Taylor estimate from the same summary holds up better. The bracket is therefore a useful early-warning signal for the quiet kind of forgetting, under a clear condition, provided the summary is kept fresh.

items.title: A counterexample to the soundness of the Flowering IOPP for codes on graphs
items.summary: The Flowering protocol of Delavenne, Medevielle and Roussel (ISIT 2025, arXiv:2501.14337) and its generalization by Delavenne and Lallemand (CANS 2025, arXiv:2508.10510) are Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity (IOPPs) for codes on graphs with Reed-Solomon local codes. Similarly to FRI for Reed-Solomon codes, the graph is recursively cut into isomorphic subgraphs and the word is folded along the cuts. We show that the soundness claims of both papers are false. The commit soundness proofs identify the vertex distance of a word to the code with the fraction of its unsatisfied local constraints, while only one inequality holds, in the wrong direction. We furthermore give an explicit counterexample.

items.title: Manipulation-resistant reputation for peer-to-peer scientific publishing: a combination-therapy approach
items.summary: In open peer-to-peer networks, where publishing is nearly free and identities are cheap, reputation systems decide what deserves attention, and their metrics become targets for manipulation. We study how to choose and combine reputation signals so that manipulation does not pay while genuine contribution does. Inspired by combination therapies in medicine, we describe each gaming action by its effects on all signals. For aggregation by the minimum of the signals, we prove that, in a global linear model, either some mix of gaming actions raises every signal by more than it costs, or the net gain of gaming is bounded by the imbalance of the attacker's honest profile; locally, gaming brings no first-order gain exactly when an admissible weighting is supported on the attacker's weakest signals. We then specify, without implementing it, MagMell, a two-tier system for peer-to-peer scientific publication: a protocol that orders signed events by Byzantine fault-tolerant consensus, enforces budgets and settles staked assessments, and open reputation algorithms that any node can run. Simulations on synthetic data show that minimum aggregation makes networks of fake identities, collusion rings and floods of generated papers lose rank beyond small intensities, at the price of a lower correlation between rank and quality for honest accounts. They also show that criticism is rarely settled, because the evidence needed is seldom available. The replicated log should grow by about 26 kilobytes per identity and year (analytic estimate), and a full recomputation of reputations takes 1.0 to 1.6 seconds for 100,000 identities (measured).

items.title: Points, Not Pixels: Keypoints, Masks and Oblique Geometry for Floating-Roof Tank Fill Estimation from Overhead Imagery
items.summary: The floating roof of an oil storage tank rests on the stored liquid, so its depth below the rim measures how full the tank is. In optical overhead imagery, this depth appears only as the crescent shadow the rim casts on the roof, often a few pixels wide. Thin shadows are difficult to measure at overhead-image resolution, and nadir-based height conversions introduce errors in oblique views. Under a local affine camera, roof depth determines the rim-to-shadow displacement through the sun and camera geometry. We regress the boundaries as sub-pixel keypoints and invert this relation with a closed-form estimator that models oblique views. Available public tank datasets do not label roof position, so we introduce SynTank-25k, 24,987 physically based renders with exact roof, shadow and camera geometry. Using the oblique estimator, the keypoint pipeline reduces fill error by $22\%$ relative to the segmentation baseline on SynTank-25k. On shadows narrower than $6\text{ px}$, its error is also lower than that obtained by converting true binary masks. Our oblique estimator reduces the error of the nadir formula elevenfold at the steepest views. On 6,558 real NAIP tank crops defined by bounding boxes, about half of the fill estimates pass internal consistency checks; NAIP has no fill labels. Data and code will be released.

items.title: Benchmarks' Last Exam
items.summary: Public benchmarks guide model selection, post-training rewards and claims of progress in artificial intelligence, yet leaderboards report aggregate scores without verifying whether each task's prompt, environment and grader agree on what counts as success. How often that agreement fails in contemporary evaluations, and in which direction confirmed defects move scores, has remained unmeasured across grading designs. Here we synthesize task-level quality reviews of 749 tasks across eight frontier benchmarks and 767 public model evaluations spanning closed-form question answering, document rubrics and agentic execution to assess whether prompts, environments and graders align. Task validity stratifies sharply by grading architecture. Closed-form benchmarks revised after public error reporting reach 92.5% verified validity, compared with 29.3% across six multi-step suites that nevertheless already supply 161 verified complex tasks. Rubric suites fail through mismatches between prompts and reference checklists, whereas execution harnesses add incomplete state assertions, shared-channel leaks and grading-time collisions. Across confirmed defects, 71.7% withhold credit from compliant solutions while 28.3% permit shortcut passes, indicating that raw leaderboard ceilings understate frontier capability on many practical tasks. Grading committed patches inside a fresh container cuts confirmed runtime bypasses from 14.7% in shared containers to 2.7% (a 5.5x drop, and 0% in read-only or static suites), showing how targeted maintenance restores existing benchmarks at low cost. As the initial milestone of the long-term Benchmarks' Last Exam initiative, this synthesis launches sustained expansion across wider benchmark coverage and deeper evaluation-quality dimensions so that pursuing leaderboard gains directly advances genuine model capability.

items.title: Automating Multi-View Quality Assessment of 3D Annotation Layouts
items.summary: Text labels provide descriptive information about elements in visual scenes. In 3D visualization, the arrangement of these labels and their connections to target locations forms an annotation layout. Assessing layout quality supports comparisons between alternative layouts. However, existing quality measures often focus on specific layout properties and may not fully reflect human judgments of overall quality. Moreover, a layout may appear clear from one viewpoint but suffer from occlusion or clutter from another. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view quality assessment method based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). We fine-tune a compact MLLM using structured supervision from human ratings to predict a rating for each quality dimension in each view. These ratings are aggregated into view-level and sample-level quality scores. To support training and evaluation, we construct the Annotation Layouts with Quality Assessment (ALQA) dataset, containing 3,216 layout samples from 1,072 3D objects across 13 categories. Each layout is rendered from 5 predefined viewpoints, and each view is independently rated by 3 human raters across 5 quality dimensions. On ALQA, our method agrees more closely with human reference scores than the evaluated MLLM baselines, and a user study demonstrates strong agreement with human preferences in layout ranking.

items.title: Sketch2TikZ: Multi-Reward Reinforcement Learning for Converting Hand-Drawn Sketches to Executable TikZ
items.summary: Automatic digitization of hand-drawn sketches into editable formats is crucial for modern document workflows and LaTeX integration. Converting sketches into executable TikZ code provides a structured representation of diagrams, but remains challenging due to noisy and ambiguous inputs, which hinder reliable interpretation and limit the effectiveness of token-level supervision for ensuring global diagram validity. To address these challenges, we propose Sketch2TikZ, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes sketch-to-code generation via a sequential multi-reward strategy, combining Code-Structure ($\mathcal{R}_{cs}$), OCR ($\mathcal{R}_{ocr}$), CleanDIFT ($\mathcal{R}_{cd}$), and Self-Similarity ($\mathcal{R}_{ss}$) rewards to enforce textual, visual and structural correctness. We evaluate Sketch2TikZ on the SkeTikZ and FlowChart-3B benchmarks using metrics including compilation success rate (CSR), image similarity, code similarity, and character similarity. Our method achieves near-perfect compilation success and improves visual and textual alignment over strong open-source baselines, while remaining competitive with proprietary GPT-based vision-language models. Extensive ablations demonstrate that curriculum-based reward scheduling is critical for reducing reward interference, stabilizing training and mitigating proxy over-optimization. Overall, our results highlight the effectiveness of reference-aware, multi-objective reinforcement learning for structured diagram generation from noisy sketches.

items.title: HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics
items.summary: Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns in continuous recordings. Repeated template reconstruction and time-pair correlation scans make analyses across brain regions, large cohorts, and parameter sweeps computationally prohibitive. We present HP-GSBS, an open-source implementation built on an exact mathematical reformulation that decomposes the matching objective into additive interval contributions from temporal prefix sums and computes Welch t-distance through constant-time rectangle queries over two-dimensional correlation prefix tables. Combined with streaming candidate search, local-window refinement, and active-block caching, this formulation drives unified CPU, PyTorch CUDA, and Triton backends. Across controlled benchmarks spanning recording lengths, feature dimensions, and search depths, HP-GSBS achieves 154- to 1,730-fold speedups while identically reproducing reference boundary histories and selected state counts (maximum $|Δ\mathrm{TD}|=1.88\times10^{-11}$). Cross-backend numerical equivalence is further confirmed on four human electroencephalography recordings from the Brain, Body, and Behavior Dataset (120--173 states). Applied to naturalistic movie-viewing functional magnetic resonance imaging from 16 participants (4,230 angular-gyrus voxels), HP-GSBS completes group and individual fits in 213.10 s on a single CPU and reveals intersubject boundary alignment above a circular-shift null (mean pairwise $F_1=0.414$ vs. 0.325, $p=0.001$). HP-GSBS reduces hour-scale benchmark fits to seconds or fractions of a second. Recording-level parallelism and an optional low-memory execution path make cohort-level and multi-timescale analyses tractable on standard laboratory hardware.

items.title: GRAML: Graph-Grounded Reasoning and Multi-Task Learning for LLM-Based Software Vulnerability Detection
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in software vulnerability detection. Existing approaches leverage program graphs to provide structural evidence for vulnerability analysis and description generation. However, redundant or weakly relevant graph relations make it difficult to identify vulnerability-related code lines and their connections to vulnerable statements. Meanwhile, generated descriptions may omit key information or contain claims unsupported by the source code. To address these challenges, we propose GRAML, a graph-grounded multi-task framework for LLM-based vulnerability detection. Specifically, GRAML uses structural propagation, relation diversity, and redundancy control to identify vulnerability-relevant code lines and their associated program relations. To improve description reliability, we further develop Tree-of-Thought-based Vulnerability Reasoning (ToT-VR), which explores multiple candidate explanations and evaluates their consistency with source code. The resulting descriptions are organized as Description samples and combined with Detection, Localization, and Assessment samples for four-task fine-tuning. We evaluated four code LLMs on seven vulnerability detection datasets. In particular, GRAML achieves average F1 scores of 67.08% to 69.32%, outperforming the evaluated baselines by 2.02 to 31.54 percentage points. Furthermore, ToT-VR improves average F1 by 4.43 to 6.99 percentage points over Chain-of-Thought (CoT)-based description generation, while multi-task training improves it by 8.03 to 18.26 percentage points over Detection-only training. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of graph-grounded multi-task supervision for software vulnerability detection.

items.title: Potential emergence in LLM agents: a statistical physics perspective
items.summary: There has been significant recent interest in understanding the behaviour of LLM agents from the perspective of human preferences or corpus statistics. In this paper we propose agent states as intermediate variables through which post-training can be measured and predicted. From a statistical physics perspective, we study the emergence of a global potential which governs the transition of state in LLM agent reasoning. We introduce a partition function to model the ideal KL-regularised transition distribution and track potential structure, mean reward and state entropy. We demonstrate our approach in two Qwen3.5-9B tasks: safety-test selection and physics-reasoning auditing. We observe that the potential structure strengthens during post-training as predicted from our framework, while joint changes in reward and state entropy provide consistency evidence. States thus provide a quantitative description of how post-training organises agent behaviour.

items.title: GAZEAIDE: Recording Gaze Context for Research on AI-Assisted Development
items.summary: Developers increasingly review code they did not write, much of it generated by AI. Where they look while reading may indicate what is relevant to them, but tools rarely have access to this information. We demonstrate GAZEAIDE, an open-source research prototype for collecting it. Using a webcam, GAZEAIDE estimates which parts of the code a developer looks at and for how long, and records this viewing history together with the text shown on screen. Such context can serve different purposes: providing visual feedback on what has been viewed, guiding code review, and preparing context for a question, which a developer can choose to send to an AI assistant. An IntelliJ plugin records work in the editor; a browser companion records assistant conversations. Attendees can record a short session, replay their viewing history, and try these scenarios.

items.title: The Times They Are A-Changin': Tracking Global Trends through the Lens of Web Search
items.summary: Human societies have always left traces of their collective priorities, from cave drawings and stone carvings to chronicles on papyrus and printed books. In the digital era, these traces increasingly emerge through social media footprints and web search behavior at a global scale. We construct the first large-scale longitudinal dataset of Google Year in Search trends, spanning 15 years, to characterize how collective public attention evolves across countries and time. Because search engines like Google and Bing do not publicly release raw search logs, Year in Search provides a rare cross-national archive of annually salient search interests. The dataset is supplemented with a manually curated, unified ten-category semantic taxonomy with strong inter-annotator agreement. We focus on four categories (Information Seeking, Personality, Entertainment, and Sports) to investigate how collective attention varies across geographic and socio-cultural contexts. Our analyses reveal a consistently glocalized structure of collective attention: countries converge strongly in profession-level personality attention while remaining differentiated in the specific individuals they search for, yet profession-level similarity is only weakly associated with geographic region and income group. Information seeking is globally dominated by politics and health, while regional distributions show varying degrees of divergence. Crisis periods are associated with both shared and regionally differentiated shifts. Entertainment and sports attention likewise combine globally prominent interests with regional differentiation. Overall, our findings suggest that web search data provide a valuable computational lens for observing collective attention at scale, acting as a living archive of how societal priorities vary across countries and change over time.

items.title: Circular Predictive Coding Unlocks Effective Depth
items.summary: Predictive coding networks perform credit assignment through an energy minimization process. Despite their ability to train models with arbitrary network topologies, they have mostly been used to train feedforward architectures to match the performance of backpropagation. However, they fail to do so when the models become too deep, because error signals become unstable or vanish as they travel through many layers. We address this limitation with circular networks, which get their depth directly from the energy minimization, rather than from stacking layers. Formally, we prove that convergence to an equilibrium of the energy functional of a circular predictive coding network approximates the fixed-point iteration process of a deep equilibrium model, showing that circularity alone suffices to unlock effective depth. Empirically, we show that circular models (i) outperform other predictive coding models of the same size on image classification tasks, matching the accuracy of state-of-the-art predictive coding ResNets and VGG networks despite having substantially fewer parameters; (ii) solve constraint satisfaction problems that require many steps of iterative reasoning, a task not feasible with feedforward models at all, reaching 99.3% test accuracy on Sudoku-hard via nested energy minimization loops; and (iii) scale to autoregressive language modeling by training a circular transformer on TinyStories and WikiText-103, before out of reach for predictive coding models. These results have direct implications for physical neural networks, where computational depth can be traded for recursion on a fixed-size circuit.

items.title: Quantum-Informed Regularized Poisson Learning for Graph-Based Semi-Supervised Classification
items.summary: We introduce IPQSSL, a quantum-informed regularized Poisson framework for graph-based semi-supervised classification under scarce labels. Local graph feature contexts are QR factorized, lifted to unitary encodings, and processed by a shared variational circuit whose measurements yield node wise diagonal weights that stabilize a symmetrized Poisson system. We establish positive definiteness of the symmetrized, regularized operator under explicit spectral conditions and derive a Hermitian, block encoding compatible formulation that separates the classical NISQ oriented implementation from a future fault-tolerant pathway. Across seven benchmarks spanning tabular data and a citation network, the effect of regularization is dataset- and budget-dependent: IPQSSL improves over the Poisson baselines on Iris and Wine at all but the single-label budget, reaching 0.946 accuracy on Iris at ten labels per class and at every budget on German Credit, where, however, all methods remain below the majority class rate. Original Poisson remains preferable on Breast Cancer, Heart Disease, Optdigits, and Cora, with the deficit narrowing as the label budget grows on the two largest graphs. Ablations attribute the gains to diagonal stabilization rather than variational training. The result is a resource transparent bridge between Poisson graph learning and quantum linear algebra, with an explicit empirical delineation of when diagonal regularization helps.

items.title: GLUT: 3D Gaussian Lookup Table for Continuous Color Transformation
items.summary: 3D Lookup Tables (3D LUTs) are widely used for color mapping, but their grid-based representation discretizes the RGB space, leading to a capacity-memory trade-off that becomes prohibitive when storing large numbers of LUTs. Recent approaches use implicit neural representations to improve scalability, but their black-box nature limits interpretability and localized editing. In this paper, we propose Gaussian LUT (GLUT), a continuous and explicit representation of color transformations using learnable 3D Gaussian primitives. By eliminating fixed-resolution grids, GLUT provides flexible representational capacity with a compact memory footprint. Its spatially localized primitives also facilitate interpretation and targeted editing. Building on GLUT, we introduce Conditional Gaussian LUT (CGLUT), a compact generator that predicts GLUT parameters for multiple LUTs within a shared framework, enabling smooth blending between color styles. GLUT further supports efficient local editing by allowing targeted adjustments to specific color regions without retraining the model. Experiments show that GLUT outperforms existing neural LUT representations in both accuracy and efficiency, while supporting controllable localized color editing. CGLUT further improves compact modeling and smooth blending of multiple color styles. Code is available at https://github.com/CVC-Color/glut.

items.title: Tasklets: A Unit-Test Benchmark for Language Model Architectures
items.summary: We introduce Tasklets, a benchmark of small synthetic tasks for evaluating the computational capabilities of language model sequence-mixing layers. These tasks probe foundational capabilities such as recall, sequence manipulation, and state tracking. Such tasks are widely used in architecture research, but differences in task selection, formulation, and evaluation make comparisons across studies difficult. Tasklets brings these tasks together, organizing them by the capabilities they test and providing a shared setup for evaluating how different architectural layer types learn fundamental computations. We compare a broad range of layer types through controlled experiments with small models. Our task implementations and evaluation code support reproducible, low-cost testing of new architectural proposals: https://github.com/zaydzuhri/flame/tree/tasklets.

items.title: Can an LLM Repair a Language Model in Weight Space Without Gradient Training?
items.summary: Although an external language model can select and test repairs to another model's weights, behavior can also be recovered through fixed numerical edits. We assessed the value of interactive selection in a controlled study of Transformer repair. After inspecting predictions, activation summaries, and weight statistics, the editor selects projection recipes to apply to the target without gradient updates. We analyzed 20 recorded sessions involving five masked and causal language models, comparing the selected edits with fixed projections, scripted and matched-budget black-box search, and low-rank adaptation. Under the core two-layer fault, live selection matches black-box search on SmolLM2 and Qwen2.5. For Pythia, live selection achieves 65.62% completion accuracy, compared with 0% for black-box search and 66.15% for a fixed projection. Under a separate compound fault affecting attention and feed-forward weights, both scripted and LLM-guided selection increase the descriptive five-checkpoint mean from 24.89% to 71.25% using the same operator family. On unmodified checkpoints, scripted projection yields small gains or losses on a separate set of framed questions. The experiments identify cases in which feedback changes an edit decision, operator coverage accounts for recovery, or supervised adaptation performs better. Combined with measurements of parameter restoration and preservation, these comparisons establish the scope of controller-guided repair for the tested faults and completion tasks.

items.title: Adapting AI Weather Foundation Models to a Changing Climate
items.summary: AI weather foundation models learn from historical archives, while the climate distribution encountered during deployment continues to evolve. This growing model--climate mismatch motivates continual adaptation without repeated full-model retraining, but the structure of weather forecast errors determines how such adaptation should be performed. We develop an online adaptation framework that exploits two complementary error structures: geographically persistent biases and flow-dependent errors that vary with the atmospheric state. Analysis of Aurora-1.3B reveals strongly concentrated forecast-loss sensitivity in its decoder, motivating flow-dependent corrections within fixed low-dimensional sensitivity subspaces. A residual memory tracks persistent errors remaining after this correction, while a variable-wise online gate controls the contribution of the persistent component. We evaluate Aurora-1.3B using ERA5 from 1959--1968 for offline initialization and a strictly chronological 1969--2022 stream for online evaluation, with updates restricted to previously available verification targets. For 2-metre temperature, distributional departure from the historical reference, measured directly from ERA5, is associated with larger frozen-model errors and greater adaptation gains, while the adapted model maintains more stable skill across evaluation periods. Across 69 output fields and five lead times from 6 to 72 hours, our method reduces MSE and MAE by 6.90\% and 6.45\%, respectively, relative to $δ$-Adapter, the strongest of six online adaptation baselines.

items.title: IsoMoE: Placement-Invariant Hybrid CPU-GPU MoE Inference with Lossless 12-bit Experts
items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity at low computational cost. Hybrid CPU-GPU inference offloads some experts to the CPU, enabling a single GPU to run MoE models larger than its memory. Expert placement changes with free GPU memory and should only affect speed. However, the greedy decoding outputs of existing hybrid engines change with placement. This is because the two devices use different arithmetic to compute experts. In addition, decoding is limited by CPU memory bandwidth. Lossless compression reduces memory traffic, but the CPU decompresses entropy-coded formats too slowly to keep up with memory reads. To address these challenges, we propose IsoMoE, an efficient hybrid MoE inference system that guarantees that its outputs do not change with expert placement. IsoMoE introduces (i) a GPU expert kernel that bitwise replays the arithmetic of the CPU expert kernel, (ii) a memory layout that allows the CPU to efficiently compute lossless 12-bit experts using AVX-512 dot-product instructions, and (iii) a dual micro-batch pipeline that overlaps CPU and GPU computation without changing the outputs. Experimental results on three MoE models show that IsoMoE produces bitwise identical outputs across different expert placements. It is also faster than the fastest baseline in every setting, achieving an average decoding speedup of 1.26$\times$ and a maximum speedup of 1.54$\times$. Our source code is publicly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/isomoe-artifact-9C21/.

items.title: Synthesizing Expressive Human-Object Interactions via Test-time Latent Adaptation
items.summary: When interacting with objects of unknown physical properties, humans sometimes probe, over-exert, stagger, and adjust through iterative adaptation instead of succeeding immediately. We argue that this process is an expressive but largely overlooked aspect of human-object interaction in motion synthesis. Both kinematic data-driven methods and physics-based controllers tend to produce flawlessly executed motions: the former lack sufficient data for learning fine-grained adaptation, while the latter use reinforcement learning (RL) and privileged object dynamics to learn robust, deterministic behaviors. We propose ExpHOI (Expressive Human-Object Interaction), a test-time latent adaptation framework built on an RL-trained physics-based control policy. During policy training, we encode diverse object dynamics contexts into a structured latent space. At test time, Advantage-Weighted Regression (AWR) iteratively optimizes the latent code for an object with unknown physical properties. Temporary mismatches between this code and the true object dynamics produce an expressive progression from tentative, error-prone trials to proficient interaction. Adaptation behaviors inevitably come with occasional failures, so a high-level planner is introduced to handle failed cases to maintain full, consistent animations. We demonstrate our framework's effectiveness on a large-object transportation task, where such adaptation is especially pronounced. To train our framework, we introduce a mass-diverse object dataset with rich physical-property annotations. Across carrying and push-pull, our method pairs over 90% success with markedly higher posture diversity, and is rated the most lifelike in our user study on animation liveliness.

items.title: PromptTTSD: Controllable Text to Spoken Dialogue Synthesis with Open-Ended Text Descriptions
items.summary: Spoken dialogue synthesis aims to generate multi-turn conversational speech from dialogue scripts while maintaining speaker consistency and contextual appropriateness. However, existing models largely lack fine-grained controllability, which is critical for capturing the dynamic, context-dependent style shifts in natural conversations. While prompt-based TTS has enabled such control for single-speaker speech, existing datasets heavily rely on predefined tags, which fundamentally limits their capacity to capture open-ended styles. To address this gap, we propose a scalable pipeline for extracting conversational speech from multi-narrator audiobooks, featuring an improved two-stage alignment algorithm to preserve dialogue continuity, paired with LLM-based extraction of style descriptions directly from narrative text. We release PromptDialog, a large-scale multi-speaker conversational speech dataset comprising 8,383 hours of Chinese speech and 120 hours of English speech, with open-ended style descriptions for 79% of utterances. We further introduce PromptTTSD, a spoken dialogue synthesis model built via a prompt-aware fine-tuning strategy that integrates style prompts into text-speech interleaved sequences. PromptTTSD is an open-source spoken dialogue synthesis model that supports both zero-shot voice cloning and natural language style control. Experiments demonstrate that PromptTTSD not only maintains strong fundamental synthesis capabilities but also achieves competitive open-ended style control compared with proprietary models, and substantially improves contextual appropriateness in multi-turn dialogues.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning Under Runtime Confounding: Policy Learning and Off-Policy Evaluation
items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly used to train robust, adaptable systems across healthcare, e-commerce, and robotics. In these settings, legal, ethical, or logistical concerns may preclude certain key variables that drive decisions from being collected during deployment time. This gives rise to a setting known as runtime confounding: the logged data hold full observability, but deployment time lacks knowledge of certain variables, known as runtime confounders. Unlike single timepoint and non-adaptive settings, runtime confounding under reinforcement learning has the potential to propagate over time, as earlier decisions affect future states, observations, and action assignments, leading to biased learning. We address these problems with three contributions: we (1) develop policy learning algorithms under runtime-confounding, (2) develop semi-parametric efficient off-policy estimation procedures, and (3) provide diagnostics for understanding the price of runtime confounding.

items.title: EssentialGIN: a new approach for gene essentiality prediction based on graph isomorphism neural networks
items.summary: Background: Prediction of essential genes (proteins), is a basic and challenging problem but at the same time very costly and time-consuming in wet-lab experiments. Predicting essential genes, only based on computational methods (to introduce wet-lab candidates) using centrality measures are not accurate and result in large number of false positives; therefore, more complex models such as deep learning and also integration of biological information are used in recent research to identify essential genes. Methods: In this work we focus on graph isomorphism networks, in order to embed proteins as a node in PPI network to conserve topological features of PPI network, and also integrate biological data such as gene expression data, gene orthology information and gene subcellular localization information, and introduced a deep architecture for predicting essential genes. Graph isomorphism network architecture is modified in this work for embedding node information. Results: Our experiments proved that the proposed method outperforms baseline centrality-based methods and also machine learning based methods such as Node2Vec, MLP, and also graph attention networks (GAT). Conclusion: In this paper we observed that using graph isomorphism networks that integrate biological data (as node attributes) and preserve network topology can significantly improve the essential gene prediction accuracy. In simpler organisms such as E. coli and D. melanogaster, methods such as multi-layer perceptron using Node2Vec embedding also performs very good, but in H. sapiens the introduced architecture significantly outperforms deep learning and other graph neural network solutions. Keywords: Essential gene prediction, graph neural network, graph isomorphism network, PPI network, node embedding

items.title: Gauge-equivariant real-space renormalization of frustrated magnets and topological spin textures
items.summary: Real-space renormalization group transformations and equilibrium Monte Carlo sampling are foundational tools of statistical physics, yet both break down in frustrated and chiral magnets. Fixed geometric coarse-graining blocks average anti-aligned sublattices and erase emergent gauge fluxes on triangular, ruby, spin-glass and multi-shell lattices, whereas local Monte Carlo dynamics suffer catastrophic topological freezing between distinct winding-number sectors below the skyrmion-ordering transition. Here we show that decimating non-adjacent spins while preserving local bond-rotation rules defines an exact-likelihood, gauge-equivariant real-space renormalization flow that overcomes both barriers simultaneously. Through exact matrix coarsening of the coupled spin network, the flow extracts a gauge-invariant frustration deficit measuring destructive loop interference, separating unfrustrated order, spin liquids and spin glasses while recovering exact Wannier residual entropy. Paired with an annealed sequence of parallel heat-bath and energy-conserving over-relaxation sweeps, the method matches thermodynamic integration to 0.01% on density-functional-calibrated fcc-Pd/Fe/Ir(111), maps its finite-temperature skyrmion melting boundary, images a 30% softening of domain-wall magnon stiffness in centrosymmetric Gd$_2$PdSi$_3$, and models experimental 219-atom ruby-lattice Rydberg spin-liquid snapshots, linking frustrated statistical mechanics to live spin-polarized quantum readout.

items.title: Formalizing Formal Semantics: The Formal Atlas
items.summary: In this paper we present the Formal Atlas, a system for the study of natural language semantics using proof assistants. Our aim is to formalize semantic accounts, check their predictions and compare the implemented theories. To this end, we connect source records and formal developments with an interactive application, where researchers can inspect proofs and modify supported Rocq files. Montague's PTQ and Gallin provide our main cases, followed by dynamic and type-theoretic comparisons, RSA and distributional semantics. We also discuss what it takes to formalize less explicit analyses. Lastly, we consider the use of AI, both for assistance in developing these resources and for inference systems that can make use of them. This work extends an earlier programme in proof-assistant semantics, with research and teaching as complementary uses.

items.title: Isonomy: Isolating Every Request from Timing Side Channels at Nearly Full-Sharing Throughput in Multi-Instance LLM Prefill
items.summary: Many long prompts share a prefix, and reusing its cached keys and values saves prefill computation. A cache hit, however, makes the first token arrive earlier and can reveal that another request used the same prefix, so providers share the cache only within an account. Under least privilege, even permission to send and pay for requests should not expose other requests' prompts in the same account. This matters because agents send unreviewed requests carrying private data, resellers pool users behind one account, and creden-tials can be stolen. Isonomy therefore isolates each request by default and lets requests opt into explicit sharing groups. Rather than give up reuse, it keeps one cache shared across accounts and hides only hits on prefixes cached outside a request's group. We target deployments where clients cannot observe one another's load, because there it suffices to hide these hits in the request's own timing. On three commercial APIs, our listeners could not distinguish added prefill work from a short request beyond measurement noise. Built on vLLM, Isonomy's gateway applies the deployment's routing rule to load and visible cache entries only, which yields the instance where the request would run if hidden hits missed. On that instance, the prediction mode estimates when the first token would be ready from the queue and the visible prefix, and gates its release. The execution mode instead reserves the work a hidden hit skips and fills it with other requests' prompts where possible. In direct-probe tests on two, four, and eight instances with every request isolated, both modes kept the upper bound on a probe's advantage within measure-ment noise at both prefix lengths. At saturation, the prediction mode retains 0.98 of unprotected sharing's throughput on two workloads with account labels, whereas isolation by account retains 0.95, or 0.80 where more reuse crosses accounts.

items.title: Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching
items.summary: Off-policy reinforcement learning of pretrained flow policies remains challenging due to the instability of optimization arising from the multi-step sampling process. Recently, Q-learning with Adjoint Matching (QAM) addressed this by recasting policy improvement as a stochastic optimal control (SOC) problem guided by a learned critic. However, QAM inherits a fundamental fragility of critic-guided improvement, since small critic errors can be exponentially amplified and often lead to performance collapse. This paper introduces Trust Region Q Adjoint Matching (TRQAM), a stable off-policy fine-tuning algorithm that adaptively controls the path-space KL between the fine-tuned and pretrained policies through projected dual descent. Specifically, we adapt a trust-region parameter $λ$ inside the sampling process of the flow policy and prove that $λ$ exactly weights the path-space KL in the SOC objective. As a result, our method can tightly control the deviation from the pretrained policy within a prescribed KL budget, achieving stable off-policy RL. Through experiments on 50 OGBench tasks, TRQAM consistently outperforms prior methods in both offline RL and offline-to-online RL. In particular, TRQAM achieves an overall success rate of 68% in offline RL, substantially improving over the strongest baseline at 46%.

items.title: Planar Formation Control with Minimal Sensing and No Common Orientation: An Almost-Global Result
items.summary: Formation control based on geometric constraints often requires either rigid interaction graphs or a common orientation reference. This paper investigates whether a prescribed planar formation can instead be achieved using only $N-1$ pairwise interactions while preserving global rotational freedom. To this end, a guiding-vector-field-inspired framework is developed in which each selected distance relation is represented by a parameterized circular manifold and the remaining geometric freedom is coordinated through relative virtual phases, based on which, a distributed controller is then constructed. The closed-loop system is shown to possess only the desired equilibrium set and a degenerate undesired equilibrium set corresponding to collapse of the central edge. The latter is proved to form a saddle-type equilibrium manifold with a measure-zero stable set, yielding almost-global convergence to the desired formation. In addition, the controller admits an implementation under mutually misaligned local frames using locally expressed relative measurements and scalar phase information.

items.title: Which papyrus HTR is good enough? Character-error-rate tolerance of four papyrological tasks on Greek texts
items.summary: Purpose: Most Greek papyri are unpublished, and handwritten text recognition (HTR) could open them to scholars. How accurate it must be for a given papyrological task is unknown. We measure the character error rate (CER) that four such tasks tolerate, with published editions as ground truth. Methods: From the 63,846 Greek texts of papyri.info we derive an error-free, letters-only transcription and degrade it to exact CERs of 1-50%. We test small models for document type, dating and documentary-versus-literary classification, trained on clean text, and eight search methods (three filters and five ranking methods). We validate the noise on real HTR output: 373 papyri unseen by the Anagnostes recogniser (889 images, 7,584 lines) are compared with synthetic twins degraded to the same CER. Results: The models keep, on average, 90% of their metric up to 20% CER for documentary-versus-literary classification, 7.5% for document type, 5% for subtypes and search, and 3% for dating. On real output (median CER 22%) the tasks lose less than on the twins: document-type classification keeps a macro-F1 of 0.82 against 0.50, and the same is seen in dating. We believe this is because real errors come in runs and leave more text intact; the thresholds are lower bounds. Conclusion: The study gives a CER target for each task, releases corpora and code, and shows that imperfect recognition is already useful for some tasks.

items.title: The Linguistic Structure of Dependency-Conditioned Embeddings
items.summary: Dependency-based distributional models capture syntactically informed lexical similarities, but the geometric organisation of dependency-conditioned lexical representations remains underexplored. We investigate the global and local geometry of lemma-dependency relation embeddings using 4 representations trained on WikiText-103: 2 count-based PPMI configurations and 2 Skip-Gram with Negative Sampling (SGNS) configurations. At the global level, we analyse dependency-relation centroids, control for lexical identity through within-lemma centring, and examine their alignment with part-of-speech (POS) distributions. At the local level, we evaluate cross-relation geometric consistency, cross-method agreement, lexical similarity, and polysemous usages. Results show that global geometry is structured strongly by the context POS across all representations. Locally, broader lexical similarity structures are partially preserved across dependency relations, while immediate neighbourhoods vary substantially, highlighting different usages. PPMI-based representations exhibit greater cross-relation consistency than SGNS-based representations, with cross-method agreement varying by relation. These findings demonstrate that dependency-conditioned embeddings exhibit systematic global linguistic organisation alongside relation-sensitive local lexical structures, with the extent of geometric consistency varying across representation methods.

items.title: Block Search Conditioned on Features for Sequential Quantum Data Encoding
items.summary: Sequential quantum data encoding is addressed through the joint selection of input features and encoding blocks within a fixed quantum register. At each step, a new feature, a block of operations, its placement, and its rotation weights are selected together from training data, extending the incremental construction of Q-FLAIR. With direct-loss selection (RAW), nine to twelve features were retained in four qubits across five new Bars and Stripes datasets. Under the same final calibration, mean changes relative to the calibrated Q-FLAIR reference were +5.53 percentage points in balanced accuracy, -15.83% in binary cross-entropy (BCE), and +7.79% in area under the ROC curve (AUC). The prespecified success criterion was met in four of five datasets and for the mean paired differences. These results were obtained by comparing complete procedures under a common cap of 32 operations.

items.title: Leakage-Free Is Not Confounder-Free: What a Patient-Level Split Cannot Certify About a Medical Imaging Benchmark
items.summary: Patient-level splitting is the standard safeguard against subject leakage in medical imaging evaluation, but it cannot remove a confounder that every fold inherits: an acquisition variable aligned with the diagnosis across the whole cohort. We present a five-question audit of a candidate confounder: how well it predicts the diagnosis, whether it can be decoded from the images, whether diagnostic scores depend on it, whether the image adds predictive value beyond it and how much discrimination survives once it is controlled. We apply it to DMR-IR, the public dataset on which most machine-learning results in breast thermography rest. On 236 patients under a strict patient-disjoint protocol, the acquisition date alone predicts malignancy at AUROC 0.980, above the best of nine imaging arms (0.949), because benign and malignant patients were recruited in different years. The acquisition year is decodable from the pixels among patients who share a diagnosis, largely through a global thermal offset outside the breast, yet only one arm, the one pooling every frame of a visit, demonstrably carries it into its diagnostic score. No arm improves on the date on paired folds, and once the date is controlled, discrimination either collapses or survives only on comparisons the benchmark cannot attribute. The dataset contains only eight cross-label same-date pairs, from ten patients, which limits reliable evaluation within recorded acquisition-date groups. A second, independently acquired cohort, whose dominant channel is patient age, returns the same audit outcome from a different confounder. Mitigation may suppress such a confounder, but without cross-label acquisition support no evaluation on the benchmark can certify that what remains is pathology.

items.title: Adesktop learning factory for smart and resilient manufacturing based on digital twin and AI
items.summary: Learning factories have been increasingly applied in engineering research and education. In this paper, we develop a small-scale, low-cost, fully open-sourced learning factory that leverages AI and digital twins to demonstrate smart and resilient manufacturing. The learning factory consists of an AGV, three robots, two conveyors and their digital twins. Three typical use cases are designed to demonstrate the capabilities of the learning factory, i.e., material sorting through computer vision-based robot control, coordinating AGV, robots and conveyors for assembly, and digital twin-driven predictive maintenance. The results show that the developed learning factory can adequately support the teaching and research activities on digital twins and AI on manufacturing. Its fully open-source architecture and relatively low deployment cost make it an ideal solution for universities and research institutions.

items.title: PRISM: Validation-Free Online Batch Selection for LLM Fine-Tuning via Preconditioned Conic Ghost Matching
items.summary: Online batch selection lowers the cost of fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) by replacing each candidate batch with a smaller informative subset. Existing selectors typically depend on a held-out validation or proxy set, or else rely on Euclidean facility-location objectives over unpreconditioned gradients whose diameter-shifted similarities are distorted by heavy-tailed gradient norms and cross-layer anisotropy. We introduce PRISM (Preconditioned Ray-Isotropic Submodular Matching), a validation-free online batch selector that aligns candidate gradients in a factored second-moment metric and casts subset construction as conic facility location over positive ray projections. Computing the required pairwise geometry through factored preconditioned ghost inner products avoids materializing per-example parameter gradients, while the conic objective remains normalized, nonnegative, and monotone submodular---guaranteeing a $(1-1/e)$ greedy approximation whose additive error scales with total batch gradient energy rather than the worst-case outlier diameter. Assigning each candidate to its best-aligned selected ray induces closed-form radial projection weights that automatically shrink orthogonal or noisy examples toward zero. We derive a nonconvex convergence bound showing that optimization error is governed directly by the conic representation cost. Across four LLM fine-tuning configurations spanning 1.5B to 8B parameters, PRISM outperforms full-batch training, Euclidean facility location, and zeroth-order selectors, and rivals or surpasses validation-guided baselines without held-out data.

items.title: Unlocking Heterogeneous Accelerator Flexibility in AI Data Centers: Sizing and Workload Allocation
items.summary: AI data centers are an emerging electricity demand, but limited local grid capacity could delay their connection and expansion. While existing operational strategies consider spatio-temporal workload flexibility, few studies address the strategic sizing and allocation of diverse accelerator archetypes with different capital and energy-efficiency trade-offs. This paper unlocks the flexibility potential of heterogeneous accelerators by jointly sizing and allocating different AI workloads (training, delay-tolerant batch work, and online inference requests) across sites and hours to meet the time-varying grid constraint at minimum cost. Workload-specific throughput and energy coefficients link these decisions to facility power. In a representative two-site case, heterogeneous sizing reduces daily cost by 6.5% relative to spatio-temporal scheduling with fixed capacity. When evaluated using workload-specific performance, a capacity design based on workload-averaged hardware coefficients costs 7.7% more than the proposed design. The proposed design also eliminates the envelope violations of an unconstrained design at a 0.25\% daily cost increase. These results show how hardware heterogeneity and workload flexibility jointly shape economical, grid-compliant capacity plans.

items.title: Plan your Self-Adaptation! Ontology-Mediated Task and Architecture Co-adaptation Planning for Robots
items.summary: Autonomous robots may need to adapt both their task plans and architectural configurations as operating conditions change. These decisions are interdependent: architectural configurations determine which actions a robot can perform, while task plans determine which capabilities are required. This paper presents PLANTA, an ontology-mediated approach to task and architecture co-adaptation that considers these dependencies during mission planning. PLANTA uses an ontology expressed in the Web Ontology Language to represent architectural alternatives and their associated functional and quality requirements, while the Planning Domain Definition Language defines task actions and mission goals. By automatically translating and integrating these models, PLANTA enables joint planning of task and reconfiguration actions. The approach uses satisficing planning and replans when changes during execution invalidate the current plan. PLANTA is evaluated in two robotic scenarios involving underwater inspection and ground navigation. The results support the feasibility of runtime co-adaptation and show lower planning time and memory consumption compared with optimal-policy generation in the evaluated navigation scenario, while producing plans of similar quality.

items.title: HistoGPA: A Context-Conditioned Gene-Prior Attention Framework for Histology-Based Spatial Gene Expression Prediction
items.summary: Spatial transcriptomics is costly, motivating the prediction of spatial gene expression from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) slides. Existing methods use tissue context to refine visual features but keep pretrained gene priors fixed across specimens. Since the relevance of such a prior may vary with tissue context, we propose HistoGPA, which conditions the gene prior itself on the slide being analyzed. A slide-level histological representation modulates a memory of pretrained gene embeddings before each spatial location queries it through cross-attention, and also gates context into the local features. Across ten cancer-specific tasks from HEST-1k, HistoGPA achieves a macro-averaged gene-wise Pearson correlation of 0.300 on the HEST-Bench genes, compared with 0.260 for the strongest of four recent methods. Capacity-matched ablations demonstrate the importance of slide-specific information and show that conditioning the gene prior provides benefits beyond visual context modulation, while pretrained gene embeddings outperform random tokens.

items.title: Minimax-Optimal Small-Loss Regret in Online Convex Optimization and Applications to Contextual Search and Online Inverse Optimization
items.summary: We give small-loss regret bounds for online convex optimization (OCO), using one subgradient per round. Let $Δ_T^\star$ denote the cumulative loss of the best fixed decision in hindsight, measured relative to the per-round minima. Our algorithm achieves the regret bound $O(1+\sqrt{Δ_T^\star})$ without knowing $Δ_T^\star$, up to domain and gradient-scale factors. The bound is minimax optimal, including its domain dependence, on $\ell_p$ balls for every $1\le p\le\infty$. No smoothness or condition bounding gradient norms by loss values is assumed, and neither loss values nor the time horizon are needed. Algorithmically, we extend the metric-update revocation of Gupta et al. (2026), originally developed for online inverse optimization, to general OCO using the follow-the-regularized-leader framework and a mixture of multiple base learners. We also apply our algorithm to contextual search and online inverse optimization. In $d$-dimensional contextual search with comparison flips of unknown bias $κ>0$, we obtain minimax expected cumulative absolute error $Θ(\sqrt{d}/κ^2)$ under Euclidean normalization using polynomially many arithmetic operations, resolving an open question of Liu et al. (2021). For online inverse optimization with the Euclidean unit-ball utility domain, our algorithm bounds the regret relative to observed actions by $O(\sqrt{d}+d^{1/4}\sqrt{D_T})$, where $D_T$ is their cumulative suboptimality; this matches the regret rate of Gupta et al. (2026) when $D_T=0$. Our guarantee extends to other utility domains; for example, on the probability simplex, the bound improves to $O(\log(d+1)+\sqrt{D_T\log(d+1)})$.

items.title: BODHI: Do LLMs Branch Out and Discover Heterogeneous Inferences?
items.summary: Although reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has improved the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), whether it expands reasoning capabilities or primarily improves sampling efficiency remains debated. In this paper, we investigate the nature of test-time exploration in RLVR-trained LLMs by employing controlled maze-solving experiments and BODHI-TREEs, a reusable representation that groups mathematical reasoning segments based on semantic equivalence. These probes help delineate preferences between stylistic variations and semantically distinct continuations. We show that RLVR-trained models exhibit lower candidate preference entropy between semantically distinct continuations than their distilled counterparts, and complementary sampling experiments show lower empirical semantic entropy and fewer observed branches under equal sampling budgets. Thus, policy concentration extends beyond stylistic choices and reduces observed semantic diversity. This reduction coexists with improved constraint adherence and backtracking in mazes, and improved recovery from distracting steps in mathematical reasoning. We conjecture that improved trace validity drives RLVR's sampling-efficiency gains, while policy concentration reduces rollout diversity. Our findings identify a central challenge for RLVR: preserving diverse reasoning trajectories alongside improved trace validity.

items.title: WEIR: Watershed Exploration and Drift-Aware Prefix Shrinkage for Multi-Turn Agent Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Multi-turn language model agents often receive only a single binary reward at the end of a long interaction trajectory, making it difficult to separate decisive decisions from routine steps or estimate accurate intermediate values. Prefix-tree methods improve sample efficiency by merging trajectories that share action histories, yet two structural flaws remain: naive pooling mixes stale off-policy outcomes into critic targets with fixed weights, and uniform or entropy-driven branching wastes continuations on dead-end states whose outcome is already settled. We introduce WEIR (Watershed Exploration and Intrinsic-Drift Shrinkage), an actor-critic reinforcement learning framework grounded in a Doob turn-variance conservation identity. WEIR maintains a cross-iteration canonical action-prefix tree with exponentially discounted visit counts and trains a prefix-conditioned critic toward a minimax drift-aware shrinkage target that adapts from single-trajectory returns at rare nodes to pooled empirical means at dense nodes. Using the same pre-update critic, WEIR allocates rollout budgets across tasks via Neyman stratification $B_q \propto \sqrt{\hat{p}_q(1-\hat{p}_q)}$ and directs within-task branches to watershed forks where high survival-headroom uncertainty coincides with steep value cliffs. Across four multi-hop QA benchmarks, ALFWorld, and WebShop on Qwen2.5-3B/7B-Instruct, WEIR achieves $32.18\%$ and $37.85\%$ average QA exact match and $84.83\%$ and $87.81\%$ ALFWorld success rates, outperforming CAPO by $1.50$--$3.74$ points while generating $28$--$29\%$ fewer rollout tokens than chain sampling.

items.title: Mjolnir: Finding and Reproducing Vulnerabilities in Root-of-Trust Firmware and RTL with Project-Grounded Agents
items.summary: A root of trust (RoT) anchors secure boot and attestation for the system above it, so a bug in RoT firmware or hardware undermines every layer that trusts it. LLM agents now find real vulnerabilities in general-purpose software, but RoT code presents two challenges. First, many security-relevant bugs depend on project-specific trust boundaries and fault-injection countermeasures rather than generic vulnerability patterns, and may cause no crash. Second, without RoT hardware, agents must exercise RoT inputs through the project's own hardware model, mocks, or RTL testbenches. We present Mjolnir, an agentic pipeline that supplies each project's threat model and design conventions to discovery and skeptical review agents, and reproduces surviving findings as proof-of-concept tests in the project's own toolchain. We evaluate Mjolnir on six firmware and RTL targets in Caliptra, OpenTitan, and OpenPRoT. On Caliptra's runtime firmware, it reaches 83.3%-100% precision across three models under blind expert labeling, including 100% on Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 66.7%-78.6% for four single-agent baselines on the same model. On 34 known security-relevant bugs in Caliptra's core firmware fixed after the models' training cutoffs, it finds 10 with Gemini 3.8 Flash versus 7 for the best baseline, and 17 with Gemini 4 Argon versus 12. Across our evaluation scans, maintainers have confirmed 64 of Mjolnir's findings as previously unknown security-relevant bugs: 37 across three models on Caliptra's runtime firmware and 27 across single scans of the other five targets.

items.title: Uncertainty-Aware Hybrid Offline Reinforcement Learning with Online Action Selection Enabled by Sparse Gaussian-Process Critics
items.summary: Start-ups and grade changes remain largely operator-driven, while developing and maintaining dynamic models for model-based control requires substantial engineering effort. Hybrid Offline Learning and Online Optimisation (HOFLON) uses one-step offline reinforcement learning to select actions from historical transition data. In its original implementation, the online objective combines the predicted return from a tree-ensemble critic with an adversarial-autoencoder (AAE) penalty for unfamiliar state-action pairs. We examine the effect of this penalty and replace the critic and AAE with a sparse variational Gaussian-process (sGP) critic. Actions maximise $μ- κσ$, an uncertainty-adjusted estimate of the return from one action followed by the historical operating practice. On the HOFLON polymerisation-reactor benchmark, removing the AAE from HOFLON led to 4 failed start-ups in 15 runs over five critics. At its published weight, the variation in the AAE penalty is four orders of magnitude smaller than the variation in the tree-ensemble critic. Nevertheless, it changes actions when the predicted returns of competing candidates are nearly equal, and paired runs with and without the penalty diverged from the first move. With a Matérn-5/2 sGP critic, $κ= 0$ led to failure in 13 of 15 runs, whereas with $κ= 3$ none of 15 runs (five critics, three noise realisations) failed. The median and lowest returns were 13,464 and 13,398 (HOFLON: 13,393 and 12,411). A squared-exponential sGP critic with learned inducing inputs needed $κ\geq 3$ to remain within the empirical data support in steady state, and then settled with a temperature offset of 2.0 K.

items.title: When evaluation becomes intervention in clinical AI
items.summary: AI judges, models that grade another system's output against a rubric, extend clinical review to the scale at which clinical AI writes. When teams use judge assessments to select a prompt or train a model, the judge becomes part of the intervention. Selection can then favor errors the judge overlooks. We describe what a judge's report must contain and the independent clinical test each judge-driven change needs.

items.title: Trilemma: How Agents choose between Honesty, Confidentiality, and Task Completion
items.summary: Personal AI agents often act on underspecified instructions and use context such as previous conversations to decide how to proceed. This context may contain private preferences that influence the assigned task or the relation to other people. When asked by a third party to justify its choices, the agent might be conflicted between honesty, confidentiality and task completion. Prior work has studied these largely as separate problems. We study deception and leakage of private information together in a simulated company Slack workspace. There, four employees delegate a sprint staffing to their personal agents. From private messages, two of these agents learn that their employee avoids working with a particular colleague. Since the agents are asked to justify their task preferences and the true justification is confidential, the agent cannot simultaneously be honest, preserve confidentiality, and complete the staffing. We evaluate 9 open-weight and closed models. Of the 135 (out of 140) open-weight agents that pursue the avoidance preference, 107 either make false claims about task fit or logistics or cite a true consideration as if it were their actual reason. Confidentiality instructions reduce disclosure of the preference from 71% (none) to 29% (medium) to 1% (strong). However, the sprint staffing is often not completed anyway, since neither agent concedes. In their reasoning, agents engage in motivated reasoning by frequently acknowledging evidence against their claims and still concluding that the claims are not false. Our results indicate that agents can make false or misleading claims in a day-to-day task without being instructed to. This environment provides a testbed for deception monitors and studying how agents resolve value conflicts.

items.title: Exploring the Potential of Ultra-Low-Bit Inference on LLM Accelerators
items.summary: Vector quantization (VQ) enables ultra-low-bit compression of large language models (LLMs) by encoding groups of values as compact codebook indexes. However, reconstructing these values for computation requires frequent codebook lookups, which conflict with the dataflows of conventional LLM accelerators and limit the performance gains from VQ compression. Consequently, prior work has resorted to VQ-specific accelerator designs, which either incur substantial additional hardware overhead or support only a limited range of inference scenarios. In this work, we argue that existing systolic-array-based LLM accelerators already possess the essential hardware resources for efficient VQ inference, but lack the mechanisms to effectively exploit them. To bridge this gap, we present VQACC, an architectural enhancement that jointly redesigns the existing operand buffer's access logic and data mapping to reuse its storage and port resources for codebook lookups, seamlessly integrating dequantization into the normal operand-addressing dataflow. Evaluation shows that VQACC achieves a 2.63$\times$ speedup over the EVA baseline, with additional hardware occupying only 0.17\% of the compute array's area.

items.title: TITAN: DRL-Based Dynamic Scheduling and Resource Allocation for Tactile Internet
items.summary: Tactile Internet (TI) applications require ultra-reliable, low-latency tactile communication alongside video traffic. However, tactile Quality of Service (QoS) requirements vary with the interaction context, making fixed resource allocation inefficient. In this paper, we propose TITAN (Two-Timescale Integrated Tactile Internet over 5G Access Networks), a dynamic scheduling and resource allocation (SRA) scheme. TITAN receives time-varying tactile QoS profiles from a higher-layer module and adapts SRA to the current QoS profile and network state. A deep reinforcement learning-based agent splits the available network bandwidth between tactile and video streams at a slow timescale, while a fast-timescale scheduler allocates resource blocks among active user equipment. Through simulations, we show that TITAN simultaneously satisfies both tactile and video QoS targets and achieves a performance gain of 7.64 percentage points (pp) in the joint satisfaction rate over the best-performing static SRA baseline.

items.title: Quadratic Gradient: Accelerating Privacy-Preserving Logistic Regression Training with Homomorphic Encryption
items.summary: Training logistic regression over encrypted data has emerged as a prominent approach to addressing security concerns in recent years. In this paper, we introduce an efficient gradient variant, termed the \textit{quadratic gradient}, which is specifically designed for privacy-preserving logistic regression while remaining equally effective in plaintext optimization. By incorporating this quadratic gradient, we enhance Nesterov's Accelerated Gradient (NAG), Adaptive Gradient (AdaGrad), and Adam algorithms. We evaluate these enhanced algorithms across various datasets, with experimental results demonstrating state-of-the-art convergence rates that significantly outperform traditional first-order gradient methods. Furthermore, we apply the enhanced NAG method to implement homomorphic logistic regression training, achieving comparable performance within only four iterations. The proposed quadratic-gradient approach offers a unified framework that synergizes the advantages of first-order gradient methods and second-order Newton-type methods, suggesting broad applicability to diverse numerical optimization tasks.

items.title: CogRec: Structure-Cognitive Fast-and-Slow Reasoning for Generative Recommendation
items.summary: Generative recommendation reformulates next-item prediction as identifier sequence generation, yet existing methods mainly treat the generated identifiers as target sequences to be memorized, leaving their hierarchical and relational structure underused for explicit reasoning. We propose CogRec, a structure-cognitive fast-and-slow reasoning framework that grounds intermediate reasoning in the same SID topology used for target generation. CogRec augments the vertical SID hierarchy with intra-layer semantic graphs and introduces SID Routing to represent recommendation reasoning through layer-wise Match, LateralJump, and Explore operations. These operations provide a structural interpretation of fast localization and slow navigation. A supervised multi-stage pipeline aligns newly introduced SID tokens, establishes direct generation, and trains natural-language and SID Routing branches from a shared checkpoint. Experiments on three Amazon Reviews 2014 categories show dataset-dependent effects of SID Routing. Routing improves Hit@10 and NDCG@10 over its direct-generation counterpart on Beauty and Sports, while reducing both metrics on Toys. These results characterize the benefits and dataset-dependent behavior of SID-grounded intermediate reasoning for generative recommendation. Code is available at https://github.com/caskcsg/CogRec.

items.title: Bringing AI Assistance to the Beznau Nuclear Power Plant: A Hierarchical System of LLM Agents for Reactor Monitoring
