For IPD studies the full multistate likelihood over linked transitions is used; for AgD studies covariate-marginal state-occupancy probabilities are computed by quasi-Monte Carlo integration of the occupancies implied by the transition intensities over the reconstructed covariate distribution, and entered through a conditional-survival likelihood. The resulting population-adjusted joint PFS/OS treatment effects can directly parameterize a state-transition economic model. On an illustrative network, ML-NMR-MS resolves a treatment's joint effect into its component transitions, separating an effect on progression from an effect on post-progression survival, and produces conditional and marginal effects. Under correct specification, a simulation study with known truth shows negligible bias and near-nominal coverage for the population-adjusted treatment effects.

items.title: Towards Fair Comparisons of AI- and Physics-Based Weather Models for Extreme Events via the Weighted Potential CRPS
items.summary: We study whether deterministic AI weather prediction (AIWP) models issue more informative forecasts for extreme weather events than deterministic numerical weather prediction (NWP) models. The deterministic model output is subjected to statistical post-processing via isotonic distributional regression (IDR), or EasyUQ, before the resulting probabilistic forecasts are assessed using weighted versions of the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS). This extends the recently proposed Potential CRPS (PCRPS) measure to focus on extreme outcomes. Since IDR exhibits optimality properties with respect to weighted versions of the CRPS, the proposed approach inherits desirable properties of the PCRPS, and, in particular, facilitates fair comparisons between data-driven and physics-based models when forecasting extreme weather events. We apply this evaluation framework to forecasts in the WeatherBench 2 dataset issued by the AIWP models GraphCast, Pangu-Weather, and FuXi, with the ECMWF's high-resolution NWP model serving as a physics-based reference. The forecast models are compared when predicting mean sea level pressure, temperature, wind speed, and precipitation extremes, defined as exceedances or non-exceedances of thresholds obtained from historical observation data. Across a range of extreme-event thresholds, including thresholds corresponding to record-breaking events, the ranking of the forecast models remains largely unchanged. We find that AIWP models, particularly GraphCast and FuXi, result in the most informative forecasts for extreme weather events across most settings, suggesting that AIWP models have the potential to outperform NWP models when forecasting extremes.

items.title: Synthetic Surrogate Functional Regression (SSFR): A Robust Framework for Estimating Spatially Varying Covariate Effects in Surrogate-Augmented Neuroimaging
items.summary: Relating demographic, clinical, and genetic covariates to high-dimensional imaging outcomes is a core problem in brain imaging, especially when the target modality is observed for only a subset of participants. Generative models can synthesize missing modalities from auxiliary data, but using synthetic images in regression requires care to ensure valid inference. We propose a two-stage Synthetic Surrogate Functional Regression (SSFR) framework for spatially varying covariate effects under partially observed imaging outcomes. By calibrating surrogate information against observed target images, SSFR improves efficiency while remaining robust to discrepancies between the surrogate and target regression functions. We establish consistency and the convergence rate of the estimator, and show that first-stage surrogate-model estimation error does not alter its asymptotic rate. We introduce a voxelwise surrogate explanatory measure $R^2(z)$, the fraction of residual target-image variation explained by a candidate surrogate; with the observation rate, it gives a principled criterion for surrogate screening and indicates the potential efficiency gain. We further develop a weighted bootstrap procedure for simultaneous confidence corridors (SCCs). As surrogate informativeness increases, SCC widths approach those obtained under complete observation, improving localization of significant effects that cannot be identified from the observed data alone. Simulations confirm accuracy and robustness under surrogate misspecification and with surrogates generated by image-to-image neural networks. Applied to spatially normalized PET images from ADNI, SSFR yields interpretable coefficient maps and uniformly narrower SCCs than an analysis using observed PET alone, enlarging the region over which age-related metabolic decline is simultaneously significant.

items.title: Elementwise Precision-weighted Compositional Data Analysis by Weighted Alternating Least Squares
items.summary: Logratio principal component is a multivariate method commonly used for exploring compositional data sets. This method is mostly used in an unweighted manner, employing the centred logratio transformation of the compositions. The smaller elements of a composition usually have a higher relative error, and can be downweighted using part-wise weighting. In this article we focus on weighting compositional data and propose elementwise precision weighting of compositions. This is particularly convenient for compositions with parts that fluctuate from rare to frequent; e.g. parts acting as traces in some samples, but being abundant in others. We suggest to weight in the logarithmic or logratio scale, with the inverse of the standard deviation of the logratio, the latter being estimated for each part of each composition separately. A weighted least squares algorithm is used for dimension reduction and compositional biplot construction. Several applications of elementwise precision weighting are described, using compositional datasets from genetics, archaeology and microbiomics that illustrate the power and advantages of a fully weighted compositional analysis.

items.title: Estimating Global Network Density from Snowball Samples
items.summary: Many analyses aim to estimate a global property of a population network, such as its density, yet only a subsample of the network is observed. Ignoring the sampling scheme, and treating the samples as complete networks leads to biased inference. Although this selection problem is generally intractable, we show that it admits an exact solution for snowball samples drawn from Erdős--Rényi networks. We derive the exact likelihood of such a sample, showing that it forms a curved exponential family in the edge probability with a low-dimensional sufficient statistic. We obtain the maximum likelihood estimator that accounts for the sampling design, alongside valid confidence intervals constructed by inverting a test based on the exact sampling distribution, via Monte Carlo simulation. Simulations show that this estimator remains unbiased even when observing as little as 0.1\% of the vertices, with nominal confidence interval coverage. We further assess robustness to departures from the Erdős--Rényi assumption using scale-free and small-world synthetic networks, as well as a real Facebook ego network. We find that, while the corrected estimator no longer attains unbiasedness under these departures, it still substantially outperforms the naive alternative throughout.

items.title: Where the Model Frequently Meets the Road: Combining Statistical, Formal, and Case Study Methods
items.summary: This paper briefly analyzes the working or default assumptions researchers in the formal, statistical, and case study traditions typically hold regarding the sources of unexplained variance, parameter values, functional forms, time, and external validity. We argue that these working assumptions are often not essential to each method, and that these assumptions can be relaxed in ways that allow multimethod work to proceed. We then analyze the comparative advantages of different combinations of formal, statistical, and case study methods, and offer advice on how to combine these methods.

items.title: Recovering Direct Price Effects of Environmental Amenities in Housing Markets: Regression and Causal Machine Learning Model Assessment with Empirical Monte Carlo Simulation
items.summary: Hedonic price models are widely used to value environmental amenities, yet practical guidance for estimating direct unconfounded price effects remains sparse. We conduct an empirical Monte Carlo simulation to evaluate traditional regression and causal machine learning (CML) approaches for estimating the direct unmediated price effect of spatially delineated amenities on treated properties (DUET), a lower-bound approximation of welfare change with direct applications to benefit-cost analysis. Whereas previous simulations rely on parametric assumptions, we preserve the actual data-generating process underlying over 1 million property transactions from upstate New York (1990--2024) and randomly assign treatment locations across iterations, establishing a ground truth against which estimation error can be measured precisely. Generalized difference-in-differences (DID) regression consistently outperforms baseline DID and two-way fixed effects models across all scenarios. Causal forest DID performs comparably to generalized DID in most scenarios and, in larger samples (at least 3,000 treated observations) increasingly common in contemporary hedonic studies, achieves significantly lower estimation error and better confidence interval coverage. Its advantage widens further when the treatment induces a nonlinear shift in the hedonic price function. The performance of causal forest DID, however, hinges on specification choices that differ from regression practice, such as including geographic attributes only in the price models and avoiding high-dimensional fixed effects. We translate these findings into method-specific best-practice recommendations for both regression and CML approaches.

items.title: Efficient inference for fairness-constrained sequential decision policies
items.summary: Adaptive decision systems in education and health choose interventions sequentially and are often required not to leave a protected group too far behind. We study the fairness-constrained optimal value: the largest population value attainable by a policy in a smooth parametric class subject to constraints that are smooth functions of group specific counterfactual functionals, such as value gaps, floors, max-min welfare and budgets. For multi-stage, non-Markov data under sequential ignorability, a sensitivity analysis of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker system shows that this value is pathwise differentiable, with efficient influence function equal to the Lagrangian combination of the influence functions of the group values. The same analysis gives the influence functions of the optimal policy, the multiplier and the group values it delivers. A cross-fitted doubly robust estimator is efficient despite its data-dependent feasible set and yields confidence intervals for the constrained value and the price of fairness. When the constraint binds, any plug-in fair policy violates the population constraint, by a margin that vanishes as the sample grows, with probability tending to one half; tightening the estimated constraint by a one sided confidence margin certifies fairness at a small cost in value. Exact checks, simulations and a synthetic case study illustrate the theory.

items.title: COMPACT: Spectral Adjustment Scores from an Exhaustive and Nonredundant Set of Invariant Relations
items.summary: Observational datasets frequently contain many baseline variables, yet investigators estimating causal effects may not know which variables to include in the adjustment set. Confounding information may also be distributed weakly across many variables. Propensity scores can simplify adjustment by reducing high-dimensional covariates to a scalar with binary treatment. Although the propensity score is the coarsest balancing score, this balancing property does not necessarily distinguish among causal structures relevant to adjustment. We instead examine all causal graphs among a candidate score, treatment, and outcome while allowing latent variables. Under faithfulness, we identify all unconditional and conditional dependence relations that remain unchanged when the treatment-to-outcome edge is added or removed, leaving treatment-effect estimation to the downstream analysis. Together, these relations define the smallest compatible graph class expressible through the relations considered. We then develop the proposed algorithm, which implements this criterion through a generalized eigenvalue problem whose score space targets the span of a treatment-balancing coordinate and a residual-outcome coordinate. We show that sufficiently informative proxies can recover this span without direct observation of the adjustment variables, characterize the resulting score-recovery and downstream causal-estimation errors, and establish bootstrap validity for the full procedure. Simulations and a real-data application demonstrate superior performance over several alternatives.

items.title: Statistical and Machine Learning Approaches for Estimating Visitation to Natural Spaces in the UK
items.summary: Natural spaces support health and well-being, but increasing recreational use can put pressure on ecologically sensitive sites. Understanding when, where and why people visit is important for planning, site management and evaluating interventions. Building on work by the Office for National Statistics, we developed statistical and machine learning models to predict visitor numbers at points located in natural spaces. We trained on automated people counter data across a range of green and blue spaces in England and Wales and tested the models' ability to generalise to unseen counter locations. Our models offer a scalable approach for predicting visitor numbers in natural spaces, reducing reliance on surveys and physical counters.

items.title: Deep conditional distribution estimation via nonparametric exponential tilt models
items.summary: Estimating the conditional distribution of a response $Y$ given covariates $X$ is a fundamental problem in statistics, underlying prediction, feature estimation, and dependence assessment. We propose a unified nonparametric representation of the conditional density, a nonparametric exponential tilt model, in which the dependence between $Y$ and $X$ is captured by an interaction function $φ(x,y)$ while both baseline densities are left unspecified. We establish identifiability and develop a nonparametric likelihood method that profiles out the baselines by empirical likelihood, with non-asymptotic error bounds under general sieve conditions. Because the profile likelihood admits no closed-form or readily tractable population counterpart, standard empirical process arguments do not apply; we therefore establish a new exponential tail bound for the supremum of a canonical U-process under a uniform entropy condition, a result we show to be new to the U-process literature and of independent interest, with a largely self-contained proof. The framework unifies several inferential tasks: mutual density ratio and mutual information estimation; a general theory for conditional features, including means, quantiles and distribution functions, without separate smoothness assumptions on the individual conditional feature functions; and a finite-sample valid permutation test of independence. Under deep neural network sieves, the convergence rates depend on the intrinsic complexity of $φ$ rather than the ambient dimension. Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method attains uniformly smaller estimation errors than existing conditional density and mutual density-ratio estimators, and delivers markedly higher power in independence testing when dependence is oscillatory or high-dimensional, while remaining comparable to established tests in standard settings.

items.title: Combining Past Experimental Data for Efficient Estimation: A Shrinkage Approach
items.summary: Firms routinely conduct randomized experiments, creating archives that could improve treatment-effect estimation in new experiments. However, past experiments evaluate related but different interventions, so their estimates may be biased for the current target. We study when and how borrowing from multiple auxiliary experiments can reduce the mean squared error (MSE) of a single treatment-effect estimate. In the oracle case, when biases and variances are known, borrowing from even one biased experiment strictly reduces MSE. In practice, we propose three shrinkage estimators and characterize their asymptotic MSE as the number of auxiliary experiments grows. Our analysis shows that average auxiliary bias and cross-study bias dispersion affect the relative performance of these estimators. As expected, smaller average bias magnitude generally improves performance. Surprisingly, bias dispersion can both benefit and harm our first estimator, the general plug-in estimator. On one hand, a more dispersed bias allows flexibility in cancelling the bias. On the other hand, the bias cancellation is imperfect as we only have an estimate of the bias, leading to overfitting. Motivated by this tradeoff, we propose a pooled plug-in estimator that restricts study-specific reweighting to limit this overfitting. However, both plug-in estimators can perform poorly when average bias is large. To address this, we develop a fixed-weight estimator with a hypothesis-testing gate that borrows only when the aggregate auxiliary mean is not significantly different from the target mean. Simulations illustrate the relative strengths of these estimators across bias environments and the relevance of the limiting analysis for finite collections of experiments. We also provide managerial guidance on which shrinkage estimator to use based on average bias and bias dispersion.

items.title: Forecast combination under temporal constraints: An application to day-ahead electricity prices
items.summary: Day-ahead electricity prices are forecast by many competing models and at several temporal granularities, from hourly prices to block and baseload products. The resulting forecasts suffer from two distinct problems: forecasts produced at different granularities are incoherent, as the aggregates do not match the averages of their components, and no single model is the most accurate in every market, period and level. We address both problems in one step by applying the coherent forecast combination framework, recently proposed for linearly constrained multiple time series, to temporal hierarchies. The resulting temporal coherent combination pools the forecasts that the competing experts produce at all the levels of the hierarchy into a single forecast that satisfies the aggregation constraints and has minimum error variance among the linear unbiased combinations. Since the optimal solution depends on a high-dimensional error covariance matrix, we compare different estimators obtained by crossing correlation structures with linear and nonlinear shrinkage approaches, and we contrast the simultaneous solution with sequential strategies. Using the base forecasts of four model classes for the German and Spanish day-ahead markets, the combined forecasts significantly outperform the base forecasts at every temporal level and are never significantly less accurate than the best reconciled expert, often improving upon it significantly.

items.title: PhiJEPA: Denoising Latent Predictions for Visual Representation Learning
items.summary: Can a predictor trained to infer hidden image regions still help a world model plan when part of an object disappears from view and the visible context is blurred? We introduce PhiJEPA, a joint-embedding predictive architecture that adapts PhiNet's two-stage prediction to masked Transformers. From sparse, photometrically corrupted context, a Transformer block predicts hidden tokens of an independently corrupted teacher view. A token-wise MLP then maps these predictions to clean teacher tokens. Controlled ablations show that the combined objective improves dense features over the tested one-stage alternatives. Pre-trained on ImageNet-1K with $5.6\times10^{19}$ training FLOPs, PhiJEPA achieves 69.3 mIoU on linear PASCAL VOC segmentation, exceeding the evaluated I-JEPA and DSeq-JEPA checkpoints in segmentation accuracy, with 25\% fewer training FLOPs than I-JEPA. It also improves hidden-region segmentation over Simple I-JEPA (49.1 vs.\ 44.3 mIoU). As an application, we use the frozen encoder in DINO-WM on PushT, and reuse the pre-training predictor, which JEPAs usually discard, to complete occluded tokens without fine-tuning. In open-loop planning with simultaneous object occlusion and Gaussian blur ($σ=2$ pixels), predictor completion raises success from 33\% to 65\%, compared with 25\% for Simple I-JEPA with its predictor and 40\% for iBOT with pixel inpainting. Together, these results support two-stage latent prediction as an efficient approach to learning visual representations that remain useful under photometric degradation and support completion under partial observation.

items.title: Verifying and Strengthening Neural Tangent Kernel Theory
items.summary: Writing Neural tangent kernel (NTK) theory explains why very wide neural networks trained by gradient methods converge in the lazy-training regime. Its standard proof combines matrix concentration, random Gram matrices, continuous-time dynamics, spectral perturbation, and a bootstrap argument, but has lacked machine-checked verification. We present a Lean\~4 formalisation for two-layer networks, proving an end-to-end theorem: for a smooth bounded activation (instantiated with $σ=\tanh$), frozen biases, paired $\pm 1$ initialisation, and explicit width conditions, gradient flow exists uniquely with probability at least $1-δ$, and $$ \|r(t)\|^2 \leq \|y\|^2 e^{-λ_0 t/2}. $$ The sole data assumption is population NTK non-degeneracy, $λ_0>0$. Initial coercivity, kernel drift, the movement bootstrap, the residual ODE, and flow existence and uniqueness are formally proved. The formalisation also sharpens the standard analysis in two ways. First, replacing the conventional matrix-Bernstein variance proxy with the classical row-covariance proxy yields estimated concentration-width certificates for $\tanh$ that are $36$--$53\times$ smaller at $(m,d)=(16,8)$ and $94$--$121\times$ smaller at $(32,16)$. Lean certifies the inequality; the ratios are numerical. Second, the network Hessian has operator norm $Θ(\sqrt{p})$ on the sup-norm parameter ball (a paper calculation), preventing the expected $O(1/\sqrt{p})$ linearisation bound via sup-norm Taylor estimates. An $L^2$ parameter geometry resolves this issue. Required widths remain polynomial but far beyond practical scales, limiting applicability.

items.title: Renewable Estimation for Generalized Nonparametric Regression with Dynamic Spline Bases and Likelihood Pullback
items.summary: A fixed spline space may limit approximation accuracy in generalized nonparametric regression with streaming data. We propose a renewable penalized-likelihood method for generalized nonparametric regression with canonical exponential-family responses. Our method combines dynamic cubic-spline refinement with Gram-metric pullback of historical score and curvature summaries. The pullback preserves the retained historical likelihood quadratic on the embedded previous spline space, while incoming data update the fit and its summaries. Under regularity and algorithmic conditions, including a growing startup and an uncapped refinement regime, we establish $L^2$-consistency at rate $O_p(N^{-2/5})$ for a fixed target in $H^2[0,1]$ and a smaller-order energy-norm discrepancy from a matched offline estimator. Simulations and applications to the Voice and Catalina datasets show that dynamic bases improve estimation when the initial representation is restrictive, with additional gains from pullback. A preliminary computational comparison also shows lower computational and storage costs than the offline methods.

items.title: Fitting the topology of synthetic particle systems with a novel graph representation
items.summary: The shape and arrangement of particles in a material determine its macroscopic properties. The generation of synthetic data with varying particle structure, often represented as 3D voxel images, combined with simulation of macroscopic properties reveals structure-property relations. Most particle generation models focus on single-particle characteristics like shape and size. We aim at fitting the topology of the particle system using tools from persistent homology. However, the large size of the required 3D image data makes existing methods computationally infeasible. We bridge this gap by introducing a novel graph representation of particle systems and transferring the computation of persistent homology from the image domain to the graph domain. This yields a postprocessing method for synthetic images of particle systems, that is independent of the underlying generation method and improves topological and geometrical agreement with real particle systems while preserving morphological characteristics such as the particle size distribution.

items.title: Inverse Probability Weighting in a Post-Bayesian World
items.summary: We present a rationale for the use of Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW) in a post-Bayesian framework, in which the bias-correction provided by IPW in a frequentist context is reframed as a retargetting of the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the statistical model and the true data-generating process. We provide a coherent argument in support of this approach, including theoretical results concerning convergence and properties of the generalised belief posteriors. We present examples demonstrating the utility of post-Bayesian IPW in practice: these include two simulated examples of inference under selection bias in the observed data, and a large-scale real-data example concerning systematic biases present in registry data when using prostate-specific antigen (PSA) to predict prostate cancer mortality. The empirical and theoretical results together show the utility of IPW to address classes of problems previously intractable within a principled Bayesian approach.

items.title: Semiparametric Efficiency for Entropic Optimal Transport under Structured Distribution Shift
items.summary: Can structural information improve estimation of entropic optimal transport (EOT), and when is the gain zero? We study a fixed-dimensional exponential density ratio model (DRM) with a nonparametric baseline, compact support, and fixed positive regularization. At positive limiting sampling fractions, an exact projection identity quantifies the variance gain from the restriction. The pooled empirical-likelihood estimator attains the restricted bound and supports asymptotically valid confidence intervals when the bound is positive. Even under correct specification, the gain can be zero and can shrink as the tilt space expands. The same projection residual determines direction-specific first-order bias under local misspecification. When both samples grow and the target fraction vanishes, a zero first-order tilt derivative can leave source fluctuations and quadratic tilt error as the leading terms. Their balance gives a phase transition in the limiting distribution. A continuous example gives different convergence rates for two correctly specified bases at the same distribution pair. Controlled experiments assess the fixed-proportion theory. Natural-data comparisons distinguish variance reductions from improvements in reference RMSE driven by smaller reference bias.

items.title: MSRyzen: An Agentic Platform for Unified Proteomics Analysis and Evidence-Centric Visualization
items.summary: Mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics is essential for comprehensive protein characterization, yet it relies on multistep computational workflows that typically demand tedious manual parameter tuning and complex software integration. Here, we present MSRyzen, an agent-driven framework that provides automated parameter optimization and extensible tool integration across bottom-up and top-down proteomics workflows. MSRyzen translates natural-language prompts into directed acyclic workflow graphs, optimizes analytical parameters guided by quantitative metrics and user-defined objectives, and incorporates new third-party software through standardized callable interfaces. Across four public top-down datasets, automated parameter optimization increased proteoform identifications by 3.6% to 15.8% compared to default settings at a 1% false discovery rate. To ensure transparent data interpretation, an interactive visualization interface coordinates identification metrics with peak-level spectral evidence and sequence coverage. Integrating adaptive tuning with multi-tiered spectral inspection, MSRyzen delivers an end-to-end, fully automated framework, dramatically reducing the operational barrier to modern mass spectrometry data analysis.

items.title: Parareal Approximation of Stochastic $L^2$-Boosting
items.summary: We study Parareal approximations of stochastic \(L^2\)-boosting, reusing the learner draws of the sequential algorithm in the fine propagators. We establish mean-square error bounds whose order improves with each correction, characterize the limiting distributions of normalized errors, including non-Gaussian components and the effects of coarse discretization, and derive sufficient conditions for preserving the statistical limit laws and validation-based stopping behavior of the sequential algorithm. Numerical experiments with sample-dependent coordinate and nonlinear residual-fitting learners examine the predicted convergence rates and limiting distributions, while computational benchmarks assess the efficiency of the method relative to sequential implementations.

items.title: What Does Matching a Human Intervention Effect Establish? Benchmark Checks for LLM Simulations
items.summary: LLM simulations are validated by equivalence with human effects, yet a zero reference passes whenever the human 90 percent interval lies inside the margin, as the human benchmark shows before simulation. When the zero reference fails, planned precision gives independent simulations the margin up to which passing is a 5 percent test of response. In an exploratory 70-experiment reanalysis, 72 percent of GPT-4's $\pm$0.20 SD passes were zero-reference passes; GPT-4 passed 16 contrasts the zero reference failed (1.58 expected without response). In a preregistered audit, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed three intention targets, all zero-reference passes, and the registered belief-gradient control; norm beliefs changed 0.065 SD against humans' 0.351 (zero-reference check added after unblinding; norm beliefs emphasized after inspection). Registered tests detected no overestimation; average-effect intervals excluded overestimation above 0.08 SD. A group audit's precision floor is 1.33 facts against a 2.9-fact effect. Report the zero-reference threshold beside every equivalence decision.

items.title: A Bayesian Distance-Weighted Ising Model for Task-Related Regional Analysis of Neuroimaging Data
items.summary: Neuroimaging analysis commonly involves identifying task-relevant brain regions and examining functional connectivity. These objectives are typically addressed separately, without a model-based framework. We propose a Bayesian distance-weighted Ising model that jointly quantifies regional importance for task-label prediction and functional connectivity between brain regions. The Ising model favors agreement between interacting labels. We extend it with region-specific interaction parameters and weights based on distances between functional signals. The parameters quantify regional importance for distinguishing tasks, while the weights measure functional connectivity through signal similarity between regions. Inference for this model is challenging because the signals may be observed on unequal time grids and the likelihood function contains an intractable normalizing constant. To address this, we use a basis expansion and an auxiliary variable Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm. We apply the method to functional near-infrared spectroscopy data from younger and older adults, comparing resting-state and task-related activity. The model reveals age-dependent patterns of regional importance and connectivity. Among younger adults, the left orbitofrontal cortex contributes more strongly to task discrimination than the dorsolateral prefrontal and frontopolar cortices, whereas regional differences are less evident among older adults. Older adults also exhibit greater bilateral connectivity between corresponding regions, consistent with reduced hemispheric lateralization.

items.title: Distillation with Errors: Sparse Unbiased Backpropagation for Knowledge Distillation
items.summary: Knowledge distillation (KD) trains a student to match a teacher's output distribution. However, full-vocabulary KD requires costly output-head backpropagation. To reduce this cost, we introduce Distillation with Errors (DWE). Our key insight is that minibatch training already approximates the training gradient, so per-position backpropagation does not need to be exact. DWE therefore exploits the zero-sum structure of logit gradients to construct sparse paired gradient estimates whose expectation matches the full-vocabulary gradient. It then uses geometry-aware pairing and stratified sampling to further reduce estimation variance. We prove that the estimator is unbiased and evaluate DWE's gradient estimation accuracy and training efficiency. At the same sampling budget, DWE reduces hidden-state and output-weight gradient MSE by 63.5% and 57.9%, respectively, compared with importance sampling. In off-policy KD, it achieves up to a $1.95\times$ output-head speedup and reduces training time by 10.4-15.7% relative to full-vocabulary KD. In on-policy distillation (OPD), it achieves up to a $2.20\times$ output-head speedup. DWE maintains competitive downstream performance in both settings. Our code is available at https://github.com/dwe-lab/DWE.

items.title: A Two-Parameter Weibull Framework for Diagnosing Transformer Weight Distributions
items.summary: Transformer checkpoints contain billions of weights, yet how their element-wise distributions vary across components, models, and training is hard to characterize. We fit the magnitude distribution of each analyzed weight matrix with a two-parameter Weibull reference model under a fixed middle-80% protocol. For i.i.d. Gaussian initialization, the corresponding half-Normal target has protocol-fitted shape $k_0 \approx 1.20$. Matched comparisons with gamma and lognormal favor Weibull for most component groups; support is less decisive for separately stored MHA query/key projections, and no tested single family cleanly describes matrices carrying a secondary weight population. Across 12 model entries spanning seven families, terminal FFN shape medians fall in a narrow band, $k \in [1.186, 1.204]$ (CV $= 0.51\%$), whereas query/key projections show architecture-associated departures. This stability is macroscopic only: in the five Pythia models whose released step-0 checkpoints permit a paired comparison, FFN and attention-output matrices remain near the reference shape despite large displacement and reorientation, so terminal shape similarity is not explained by parameter proximity alone. The fitted shape $k$ is read as a reference-relative central-body shape indicator and the scale $λ$ as a magnitude coordinate; neither is presented as a predictor of downstream performance. In a Qwen case study, the screen localizes a shallow-FFN secondary small-magnitude population, and direct raw-weight analysis of a flagged block traces much of that population to coherently suppressed intermediate channels. The method requires only released checkpoints and complements behavioral and structural analyses. The code and reference database are available at https://github.com/tiexinding/NPM-Weibull-public.

items.title: Reliable Behavior Discovery via False Discovery Rate Control
items.summary: Reliable methods for discovering behavior patterns in large generative models are increasingly essential as models become both more complex and capable. We formalize behavior discovery as a problem class of interest and highlight the task of controlling false discovery rate (FDR) as crucial for guaranteeing reliability in behavior discovery. Building upon the multiple hypothesis testing literature, we propose DISCO (Discovery through Iterative Search with COarsened $e$-processes), a method which provably controls FDR in behavior discovery under mild conditions. DISCO improves power over previous related eBH-based approaches by allowing for adaptivity to a data-dependent number of hypotheses to be tested. We demonstrate empirically that DISCO controls FDR with higher power than comparable approaches on both synthetic data and a novel empirical evaluation of FDR-controlling methods in settings where large generative models act as both discovery engines and targets. Code is available at https://github.com/google-deepmind/disco .

items.title: A bivariate cure copula model with zero-inflated gamma frailty for right-censored data
items.summary: In biomedical studies, paired survival data arise naturally when two event times are observed within the same subject. Existing statistical models seldom accommodate both cure fractions and complex dependence structures. In this paper, we propose a novel bivariate cure frailty-copula model for paired survival data with a cure fraction. By incorporating a zero-inflated gamma frailty, the proposed framework simultaneously accommodates a cure fraction and continuous unobserved heterogeneity among uncured subjects. Dependence between cure statuses is modeled naturally via an odds-ratio parameter, while dependence between survival times conditional on frailty is captured through a copula. To provide interpretable measures of overall dependence in the presence of cure, we derive population-level rank correlation coefficients, namely tie-adjusted versions of Kendall's tau and Spearman's rho. For suitable choices of baseline marginal survival functions and copulas, the joint survival function admits a closed-form expression, enabling maximum likelihood estimation and likelihood ratio testing. Simulation studies demonstrate satisfactory finite-sample performance and favorable comparisons with existing bivariate cure models. In a real-data analysis, the proposed model is favored by information criteria. An R package, curecopula, implementing the proposed methods is publicly available on GitHub.

items.title: graphMTP: An R Shiny Interface for Graphical Multiple Testing and Interim Monitoring
items.summary: Graphical multiple testing procedures provide a framework for controlling the family-wise error rate across endpoints, treatment comparisons, and patient populations in confirmatory clinical trials. Interim monitoring requires analysts to track changing local significance levels together with hypothesis-specific testing schedules. We present graphMTP, an R application built with shiny, for constructing hypothesis graphs, specifying per-hypothesis group-sequential plans, and inspecting alpha recycling. The application uses TrialSimulator for graph updates, gsDesign for spending profiles, and rpact for boundary calculations. It records the local levels, boundaries, and decisions used for each submitted test and exports designs and histories as JSON files. Worked examples cover fixed-design reallocation, fixed-sequence gatekeeping, delayed activation, and retesting a previously monitored recipient of alpha. Replication code checks graph updates, normal crossing probabilities, and saved-session replay. Sequential tests use a prespecified information schedule and reconstruct the complete local boundary family at the current allocation, including after recycling. Historical event records retain the boundaries actually used. An installable package and standalone sources accompany the article.

items.title: Inference in High-Dimensional Linear Mediation Models
items.summary: Mediation analysis plays an important role in psychology, epidemiology, and genomics. Al- though high-dimensional mediation has been studied extensively, existing inferential methods typically rely on sparsity assumptions that may be difficult to justify when many individually weak mediators collectively produce a substantial effect. We study inference for both the over- all indirect effect and the effect transmitted through an individual mediator in a proportional high-dimensional regime, where the number of mediators and the sample size grow at compa- rable rates, without imposing sparsity on the mediator effects. Standard debiasing procedures for high-dimensional inference commonly rely on design-covariance information or additional structural assumptions on precision-matrix directions. In mediation models, however, the full outcome-design covariance depends on unknown mediator-model coefficients, creating an addi- tional challenge when such information or structure is unavailable. To address this challenge, we introduce an approximate debiasing procedure based on partial ridge regression and show that the resulting estimator is asymptotically bias-corrected and Gaussian. We also develop a cross-fitted estimator with a smaller asymptotic variance than its sample-split counterpart. In addition, we construct consistent estimators of the limiting variances of both the sample-split and cross-fitted estimators. Together, these results provide feasible inferential procedures for global and pathwise mediation effects.

items.title: Deep Learning-based Approaches for State Space Models: A Selective Review
items.summary: State-space models (SSMs) offer a powerful framework for dynamical system analysis, wherein the temporal dynamics of the system are assumed to be captured through the evolution of the latent states, which govern the values of the observations. This paper provides a selective review of recent advancements in deep neural network-based approaches for SSMs, and presents a unified perspective for discrete-time deep state space models and continuous-time ones such as latent neural Ordinary Differential and Stochastic Differential Equations. It starts with an overview of the classical maximum likelihood based approach for learning SSMs, reviews the variational autoencoder as a general learning pipeline for neural network-based approaches in the presence of latent variables, and discusses in detail representative deep learning models that fall under the SSM framework. Very recent developments, where SSMs are used as standalone architectural modules for improving efficiency in sequence modeling, are also examined. Finally, we present examples involving nowcasting and irregularly sampled time-series data, together with a brief overview of scientific applications based on mechanistically structured SSMs.

items.title: A General Framework for Metropolis-Adjusted Dikin Walks: Dimension-Square Mixing on Polytopes and Log-Det Walks on Spectrahedra
items.summary: Sampling from a log-concave density over a convex body is a fundamental problem. The Metropolis-adjusted Dikin walk draws Gaussian proposals shaped by a local barrier metric, and the main difficulty in its analysis is to control the proposal determinant and the reverse quadratic form at a random endpoint. In this paper, we analyze these walks with exact metrics by keeping the two terms together. In the complete logarithmic acceptance ratio, their leading uncentered terms cancel, and second-order tools control the remaining centered fluctuations. For a polytope given by $n$ inequalities and a convex $L$-Lipschitz potential, we show that the regularized Lee--Sidford walk mixes from a warm start in $\widetilde O((d^{2}+dL^{2}R^{2})\log(w/δ))$ steps. For a spectrahedron with $n\times n$ blocks, we show that the log-det walk scaled by $κ=\widetilde O(ψ^\star)$ mixes in $\widetilde O((ψ^\star nd+dL^{2}R^{2})\log(w/δ))$ steps, where $ψ^\star$ measures matrix leverage. Both analyses share an acceptance-to-mixing reduction. Moreover, we give exact-arithmetic implementations. For polytopes, a proposal-comparison argument transfers the bound to an appropriately padded $O(1/d)$-accurate metric computed from high-precision Lewis weights. For spectrahedra, given $\widehatψ\geψ^\star$, our implementation with the exact or a TensorSRHT-sketched log-det metric obtains the same bound with $ψ^\star$ replaced by $\widehatψ$.

items.title: Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting: Robust Inference under Deterministic and Random Distribution Shifts
items.summary: Reweighting source samples to match a target covariate distribution is a standard response to distribution shift when generalizing evidence across populations. It is well suited to deterministic, learnable covariate discrepancies, but can fail when source--target differences extend beyond covariate shift or when estimation of the density-ratio weights is unstable. We introduce a new model where the discrepancy between two population laws comprises a deterministic covariate shift and a non-systematic component, modeled as random perturbation of the probability space. This separates systematic shifts, treated as bias and corrected by reweighting, from random perturbations, treated as distributional uncertainty and reduced by dataset pooling. Under pure random perturbations, this principle yields Augmented Inverse Distance Weighting, which combines regression augmentation with variance-optimal dataset-level pooling and attains asymptotic variance no larger than exact covariate balancing. When both components are present, we develop Augmented Inverse Hybrid Weighting, which interpolates between AIDW and standard augmented importance weighting. Both estimators tradeoff sampling and distributional uncertainty via a distributional distance quantifying the strength of random perturbations. We establish asymptotic normality of both estimators and provide tuning and diagnostic tools. On three real-world multi-site datasets exhibiting diverse distribution shifts, the proposed methods consistently reduce mean-squared error compared with weighting baselines, and improve empirical coverage when covariate-shift adjustment alone undercovers.

items.title: Beware of complexity bias: A hindrance to conceptual model generalization and interpretability
items.summary: In the field of rainfall-runoff modeling, lumped conceptual models have been shown to be powerful representations of catchment filtering functions. They demonstrate fairly strong predictive performance in gauged catchments and have the ability to learn important intermediate latent variables and flow paths which increases their value as interpretable models. During calibration, these conceptual models may fit streamflow just as well as deep learning models, however, their performance often sharply degrades after deployment, suggesting the presence of overfitting. We hypothesize that complexity (or flexibility) bias is one of the causes of such overfitting. Complexity bias can appear within conceptual models when the number of effective degrees of freedom is parameter or flow path dependent. Using a popular conceptual model and a series of synthetic datasets, we illustrate the presence of complexity bias and demonstrate its impact on model interpretability/parameter inference. Then, using real rainfall-runoff data from CAMELS-US, we investigate if overfitting can be reduced by adding regularization terms that prevent complexity bias from forming. Our results suggest that conceptual and hybrid modeling can be further improved if hydrologists become aware of this pervasive bias.

items.title: Subspace Inference for Multilayer Latent Space Networks: Intrinsic Geometry and One-Step Estimator
items.summary: Multilayer networks on a common node set, such as brain connectomes of several animals with one layer per animal, often share a low-dimensional geometry but differ in how strongly each layer expresses it and in node activity. We study a multilayer latent space network model that combines an invariant subspace common to all layers with layer-specific interaction matrices and node-by-layer degree effects. By introducing the generalized Cayley transform of the invariant subspace, we characterize the intrinsic geometry of the model and obtain sharp convergence rates for the maximum likelihood estimator, asymptotic normality and Neyman orthogonality for vertex-level parameters, and asymptotic normality for the interaction matrices with a non-negligible bias. Plug-in estimates of the bias and covariance give debiased confidence regions and tests of equality between layers. We also propose an easy-to-implement one-step estimator that attains the same vertex-level limits. In a real-world mouse connectome dataset, the inbred strain that lacks a corpus callosum shows about twice the hemispheric segregation of the other three strains.

items.title: Average Causal Effect Estimation in DAGs with Hidden Variables: Beyond Back-Door and Front-Door Criteria
items.summary: The identification theory for causal effects in directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) with hidden variables is well established, but methods for estimation and inference beyond the g-formula remain less developed. Previous studies have introduced influence-function-based estimators for broad classes of identifiable effects. When implemented through the observed-data density factorization, these estimators can require conditional density estimation and numerical integration, which can be statistically challenging and computationally demanding for continuous or multivariate variables. Prior work on related causal functionals has used sequential regressions and Bayes-rule representations of density ratios to avoid these requirements. Building on established identification and influence-function results, we make these reparameterizations explicit for effects identified under treatment primal fixability, Tian and Pearl's necessary and sufficient condition for identification of post-intervention law, encompassing settings beyond classical back-door and front-door identification. We construct one-step estimators under alternative nuisance parameterizations and characterize how these choices affect robustness properties and nuisance-specific L2(P) product-rate conditions for asymptotic linearity and root-n consistency. The estimators accommodate data-adaptive machine learning for nuisance estimation. To address potential violations of the target parameter bounds by one-step estimators, we also develop targeted minimum loss-based estimators (TMLEs) that respect these bounds. Our robustness characterizations and sufficient rate conditions apply to both the one-step estimators and TMLEs. Building on prior efficiency theory for hidden-variable DAGs, we further develop modifications of our estimators that exploit ordinary independence restrictions. Implementations are provided in the R flexCausal package.

items.title: Randomization Tests in Randomized Saturation Designs
items.summary: Randomized saturation designs are widely used to study spillover effects in clustered populations. In these designs, clusters are first assigned to treatment saturation levels, and units are then randomized within clusters according to the assigned saturation. This paper develops randomization tests for such experiments under several null hypotheses that arise naturally in spillover analysis. We first compare each unit's untreated potential outcomes at two saturation levels: the partially sharp null requires zero spillover for every unit, while the bounded null imposes a prespecified upper bound on each unit's spillover effect. Both hypotheses can be tested using a common conditional randomization framework that provides finite-sample validity. We next develop a finite-sample valid unconditional randomization test of whether each unit's untreated potential outcome is nondecreasing across saturation levels. Finally, we study weak average-spillover nulls and show that our conditional randomization framework delivers asymptotically valid inference using studentized statistics. Simulations and an application to the Zomba Cash Transfer experiment illustrate the finite-sample behavior and practical implementation of the methods.

items.title: Beyond Arrow: From Impossibility to Possibility in Multi-Criteria Benchmarking
items.summary: Modern benchmarks such as HELM MMLU account for multiple metrics like accuracy, robustness and efficiency. When trying to turn these metrics into a single ranking, natural aggregation procedures can produce cyclic pairwise comparisons or rankings that are unstable to changes in the model set. We formalize this aggregation as a social choice problem where each metric induces a preference ranking over models on each dataset, and a benchmark operator aggregates these votes across metrics. While prior work has focused on Arrow's impossibility result, we identify sufficient conditions under which the impossibility disappears and meaningful multi-criteria benchmarking becomes possible. In particular, we deal with three restrictions on the combinations of rankings and show that on single-peaked, group-separable and distance-restricted preferences, the benchmark operator allows for the construction of well-behaved rankings of the involved models. Empirically, we investigate several modern benchmark suites like HELM MMLU and verify which structural conditions are fulfilled on which benchmark problems.

items.title: A generalized Bayesian method for identifying local and global changepoints in dynamic network data
items.summary: We introduce a generalized Bayesian approach to multiple changepoint analysis in dynamic network data based on a multinomial log loss function and a prior distribution that imposes low-rank structure and sparsity on the model parameters. The method can detect local and global changes in network structure by incorporating information from both the full adjacency matrices and network summary statistics. Moreover, the proposed method is agnostic to the true data-generating process. From the generalized posterior distribution, we can make simultaneous inferences with meaningful uncertainty quantification about the locations of changepoints as well as deduce the network attributes and summary statistics that characterize them. For posterior simulation, we develop an efficient Gibbs sampler based on Pólya-Gamma data augmentation with a computational cost that grows linearly with the number of observed edges in the dynamic network. Simulations across several benchmark network models show that the proposed method is often more accurate and flexible than competitors. We demonstrate the practical value of the method through applications to an email communication network and an international conflict network.

items.title: Spectral Estimation with Deformed Decompression
items.summary: Sample covariance matrices are fundamental objects in machine learning and statistics, with valuable information encoded into their eigenvalues. When treating modern problems, the scale of these matrices can become prohibitive for tractable computation. This creates a critical need for "spectral decompression": a method for inferring the eigenspectrum of a very large-scale model using only information from its smaller realizations. Existing methods fall into two main categories: those relying on spectral inversion; and those that rely on Free Decompression techniques. On the one hand, spectral inversion is a fundamentally ill-posed problem that is notoriously unstable, often failing to yield reliable results in finite-size settings. On the other hand, while Free Decompression was recently proposed to address this scaling, its reliance on the Nica-Speicher framework restricts its use to unitarily invariant ensembles, a symmetry condition that subsampled covariance matrices fail to satisfy. In this work, we introduce Deformed Decompression (DD), a novel framework for the stable, forward-extrapolation of spectral densities. By leveraging properties of the companion matrix, DD recasts the spectral decompression problem as a directed evolution of the Stieltjes transform of the companion matrix. This approach bypasses the instabilities of traditional inversion and provides a robust methodology for scaling covariance matrices and even their generalized variants (including Hessian matrices) that lack unitary invariance. We demonstrate the utility of our framework through experiments on a variety of random matrix examples, showing that DD successfully captures the complex spectral signatures of large-scale systems.

items.title: MG-EDA: Maturity-Gated Skew-Normal Estimation of Distribution Algorithms
items.summary: Gaussian estimation of distribution algorithms shrink their variance on slopes and stall far from the optimum. This paper equips the corrections that act along the direction of movement -- a mean shift, an elongation of the covariance along the path and a skewness -- with the rule they lack: a calibrated gate, driven by a maturity statistic of the population, decides whether, how strongly and for how long each correction acts, and when the gate is closed the algorithm is exactly the estimation of multivariate normal algorithm (EMNA). The statistic is a cumulative path of whitened mean shifts with an inverse-Wishart correction, whose expectation is one under a null model without systematic movement and whose quantiles give thresholds with known false-alarm rate. It gates the three corrections as three rank-one terms of one matrix sampling equation, the skewness being carried by a skew-normal sampler that preserves the estimated mean and covariance; all vanish at maturity. We call the resulting algorithm the maturity-gated EDA (MG-EDA). A full factorial study on a training set of black-box optimization benchmarking (BBOB) functions separates the parameters: variance scaling is the prerequisite, the mean shift needs a feedback correction removing the injected shift from the statistic, the elongation turns the variance loss on a slope into a gain, and the skewness substitutes for the mean shift rather than complementing it. On held-out instances MG-EDA with the first- and second-order corrections is significantly better than the skewness-only predecessor and than EMNA with variance scaling, ties with EMNA with anticipated mean shift, and trails the adapted maximum-likelihood Gaussian model (AMaLGaM) in 20 dimensions.

items.title: Free Decompression with Algebraic Spectral Curves
items.summary: Tools from random matrix theory have become central to deep learning theory, using spectral information to provide mechanisms for modeling generalization, robustness, scaling, and failure modes. While often capable of modeling empirical behavior, practical computations are limited by matrix size, often imposing a restriction to models that are too small to be realistic. This motivates the inference of properties of larger models from the behavior of smaller ones. Free decompression (FD) is a recently proposed method for extrapolating spectral information across matrix sizes, but its utility is currently limited by strong assumptions that preclude its implementation on more realistic machine learning (ML) models. We use algebraic spectral curve theory to provide a general FD methodology for spectral densities whose Stieltjes transform satisfies an algebraic relation, a modeling assumption that is more likely to hold in practice. This recasts FD as an evolution along spectral curves which can be readily integrated. Our framework enables the expansion of spectral densities that have multiple or multi-modal bulks, that exist at multiple scales, and that contain atoms, all characteristic of real-world data and popular ML models. We demonstrate the efficacy of our framework on models of interest in modern ML, including Hessian and activation matrices associated with neural networks and large-scale diffusion models.

items.title: Large Reported CHB-MIT Adaptation Gains Disappear with Pretrained Encoders and Matched Probes
items.summary: Dani and Liebe (2026) (DL) report that adapting the final encoder block of BIOT and CBraMod with self-supervised learning (SSL) improves CHB-MIT seizure-detection ROC-AUC by 36.2 and 29.5 points over linear probing. We investigate these results with their released code and an independent pipeline. The release loads pretrained weights for adaptation only when an otherwise unset configuration key is supplied, and its CBraMod probe reads the reconstruction head with dropout active. With pretrained initialisation and a probe on the encoder output in evaluation mode, the fixed-recipe adaptation gain on DL's split is -0.6 points for BIOT (95% interval [-3.8, +2.6]) and +0.01 for CBraMod ([-0.02, +0.04]) across five seeds. Across DL's split and five subject rotations on CHB-MIT and Siena Scalp EEG, with equally tuned linear probes (30 configurations, up to 500 epochs, validation-based early stopping), mean adaptation effects range from -1.1 to +5.7 ROC-AUC points over 18 comparisons (related settings and feature variants). Twelve of 18 support equivalence within +/-3 points under dependence-adjusted inference (8 of 12 rotation and 4 of 6 fixed-split comparisons); six are unresolved. After correcting rotation intervals for dependence, no positive effect has a 95% interval excluding zero. The +/-3 margin is an analysis threshold, not a clinically validated one, and smaller margins support fewer equivalences. Two fixed-probe gains near +21 points shrink under the same tuning, with smaller benefits unresolved. We also audit a CHB-MIT protocol shared by at least 14 papers. No tested configuration reproduces DL Table 1 as a whole. These findings concern the tested configurations; the encoder-level probe and subsequent checks were chosen post hoc.

items.title: Uncovering Multimorbidity Patterns Through a Novel Randomized Clustering Algorithm
items.summary: Patients with several chronic conditions rarely share the same combination: in four years of the nationally representative Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), we find 32,789 distinct combinations of two to seven conditions, and over 90% of those involving four or more occur in a single patient. Methods that search for common combinations discard most of this heterogeneity. We present the Randomized Length Sequential Clustering Algorithm (RLSCA), which links diseases by lift, a pairwise association measure counted only above a user-set support threshold. A mixed-integer program repeatedly selects and removes the group of conditions with the greatest internal lift, up to a random size; 100 iterations yield a database of clusters scored by size, rediscovery frequency, and body systems spanned. In MEPS 2019, stratified by age and sex, RLSCA recovers known groupings at a high threshold, such as diabetes with lipid disorders and hypertension, and at a lower threshold returns clusters of up to eight conditions spanning five body systems. Frequent itemset mining, at its lowest feasible support, finds no set above five conditions; hierarchical clustering cannot control cluster size. With a clinical large language model, the database could suggest which further conditions a patient is at risk of.

items.title: Random weighting inference for linear regression under serial dependence of unknown form
items.summary: We construct confidence regions for a linear regression's coefficients, with regressors and errors forming a stationary ergodic sequence of serial dependence not necessarily known. We weight the observations by random variables from an independent auxiliary sample and estimate the coefficients by weighted least squares. We prove the estimator to be asymptotically normal with the sandwich covariance if and only if the bandwidth shrinks fast enough for the weights' randomness to dominate the score's serial dependence. Wald regions have the nominal level, under short memory with the dependence left unspecified and under long memory with a non-normal least-squares limit. We derive a condition specific to the slopes and a bandwidth from consistent memory-order estimates, and identify the estimator asymptotically with least squares perturbed by independent noise. In simulations, we compare our regions with self-normalized, fixed-bandwidth, and resampled intervals under short and long memory, and we apply the method to daily wind speeds at Irish stations, a long-memory series.

items.title: Estimating a Rational Inattention Discrete Choice Model: A Semiparametric Approach
items.summary: People's choices depend on both the payoffs of the available options and what they learn about those payoffs before deciding. This paper shows how choice data identify both unobserved payoff heterogeneity and the cost of information acquisition in a rational inattention discrete-choice model. I establish conditions for semiparametric point identification using exogenous payoff and information-cost shifters, without imposing parametric forms on the taste-shock distribution or on how the unit cost of information varies with observed characteristics. In the model with binary choice, I construct an unobserved choice threshold whose cumulative distribution function is the choice probability as a function of the payoff shifter. Moments of this threshold identify the payoff coefficients and the unit cost of information at each value of the information-cost shifter. A deconvolution argument then identifies the taste-shock distribution. I then extend identification to the model with multinomial choice. To estimate the model, I propose a sieve minimum-distance estimator based on observed market shares and establish its consistency. For inference, I construct confidence regions by test inversion because binding parameter constraints can make the estimator's limiting distribution nonnormal. In an application to Amazon Mechanical Turk, model counterfactuals show that lower unit costs of information raise the average task-taking probability and reduce wage elasticity.

items.title: Estimating conditional means under missingness-not-at-random with incomplete auxiliary variables
items.summary: Estimators assuming missingness at random (MAR) can fail under missingness not at random (MNAR). Introducing complete auxiliary variables sometimes restores MAR by breaking dependence between analysis variables and missingness. However, if the auxiliaries are themselves incomplete, MAR typically remains violated. We derive necessary and sufficient, weaker-than-MAR conditions under which the MAR functional $μ_{\rm MAR}$ for a conditional mean $E[Y \mid X]$ is correct. We also propose an alternative identifying functional for $E[Y \mid X]$, called $μ_{\rm MIA}$ for "Marginalization over Incomplete Auxiliaries", along with sufficient conditions for $μ_{\rm MIA}$ to be correct. For MNAR distributions in which all missingness patterns can occur and certain context-specific independences do not occur, there are two straightforward cases where $μ_{\rm MIA}$ is correct for a strict superset of the MNAR distributions for which $μ_{\rm MAR}$ is correct: (1) $X$ is complete and $Y$ is incomplete; or (2) all auxiliary variables are incomplete. In case (1), $μ_{\rm MAR}$ is always incorrect, barring knife-edge cases. Determining whether either case holds requires no knowledge of the MNAR mechanism. We propose estimators of $μ_{\rm MIA}$, including g-computation and doubly robust estimators. Our R package miapack implements a semiparametric iterated-conditional-expectations estimator. We illustrate with real data and present simulations comparing estimators of $μ_{\rm MIA}$ and $μ_{\rm MAR}$.

items.title: Efficient Subgroup Analysis via Optimal Trees with Global Parameter Fusion
items.summary: Identifying and making statistical inferences on differential treatment effects (commonly known as subgroup analysis in clinical research) is central to precision health. Subgroup analysis allows practitioners to pinpoint populations for whom a treatment is especially beneficial or protective, thereby advancing targeted interventions. Tree based recursive partitioning methods are widely used for subgroup analysis due to their interpretability. Nevertheless, these approaches encounter significant limitations, including suboptimal partitions induced by greedy heuristics and overfitting from locally estimated splits, especially under limited sample sizes. To address these limitations, we propose a fused optimal causal tree method that leverages mixed integer optimization (MIO) to facilitate precise subgroup identification. Our approach ensures globally optimal partitions and introduces a parameter fusion constraint to facilitate information sharing across related subgroups. This design substantially improves subgroup discovery accuracy and enhances statistical efficiency. We provide theoretical guarantees by rigorously establishing out of sample risk bounds and comparing them with those of classical tree based methods. Empirically, our method consistently outperforms popular baselines in simulations. Finally, we demonstrate its practical utility through a case study on the Health and Aging Brain Study Health Disparities (HABS-HD) dataset, where our approach yields clinically meaningful insights.

items.title: Estimating contextual networks via Fisher-scoring surrogate likelihood
items.summary: When networks are accompanied by vertex-level covariates, effectively integrating and aligning the information underlying both data sources becomes a natural yet critical task. Current spectral approaches, despite their popularity, may yield suboptimal results and necessitate the specification of additional tuning parameters that are contingent upon unobservable signal-to-noise ratios. We propose a tuning-free, likelihood-based learning framework for estimating latent positions in contextual generalized random dot product graphs in the presence of high-dimensional vertex covariates with a low-rank structure. Our method constructs a smooth surrogate likelihood and implements a Fisher-scoring algorithm to iteratively estimate latent positions without introducing additional tuning parameters that depend on the network sparsity. We establish the consistency and asymptotic normality of the Fisher-scoring estimator. Application to real-world data further demonstrates the method's practical utility, offering a principled and scalable alternative to spectral approaches for analyzing contextual networks in high-dimensional settings.

items.title: Semiparametric Double Reinforcement Learning with Applications to Long-Term Causal Inference
items.summary: Double reinforcement learning (DRL) provides efficient off-policy inference for policy values in nonparametric Markov decision processes (MDPs), but fully nonparametric estimators can be unstable when intertemporal overlap is weak and occupancy ratios are high-dimensional. This limitation is especially relevant for long-term causal inference from randomized experiments: randomization ensures overlap in treatment assignment, but not over future state trajectories induced by continued intervention use. We develop semiparametric DRL for continuous linear functionals of the infinite-horizon $Q$-function. Rather than impose linear MDP structure on the reward and transition laws, we place working semiparametric restrictions on the $Q$-function itself, the solution of the discounted Bellman equation. When correct, these restrictions can improve efficiency relative to unrestricted DRL while allowing rich, possibly infinite-dimensional models. To avoid relying on correct specification, we define the estimand through weighted Bellman-residual minimization. The resulting projection target remains meaningful under misspecification and recovers the original functional under correct specification. For this class of parameters, we derive efficient influence functions and efficiency bounds, construct model-robust automatically debiased estimators, and develop minimax criteria for estimating the $Q$- and Riesz functions. Under correct specification, optimally weighted versions attain the semiparametric efficiency bound in the restricted model.

items.title: A Deep Zero-Inflated Model of North Atlantic Right Whale Presence To Support Blue Economy Management
items.summary: Effective modeling of endangered marine mammal species, such as the North Atlantic Right Whale, is critical for balancing marine conservation with the growing blue economy. Passive acoustic monitoring data collected by autonomous underwater vehicles provide new opportunities for localized marine species detection and oceanographic sensing, but introduce complex statistical challenges such as zero inflation, imperfect detection, and intricate dependence structures. In response, we propose the Deep Zero-Inflated Bernoulli (DeepZIB) model, a deep statistical method which jointly models latent species presence and conditional detection probabilities while learning complex habitat relationships from heterogeneous covariate information. We establish theoretical results on the model's structural properties and conduct simulation experiments to demonstrate its ability to recover underlying parameters and latent presence fields. Application to real-world passive acoustic monitoring data on the North Atlantic Right Whale along the U.S. East Coast demonstrates improved model adequacy and predictive performance in capturing the species' dynamic and spatially varying habitat. We demonstrate DeepZIB's ability to generate high-resolution, spatially and temporally varying presence maps, providing valuable insights for targeted and risk-aware management of blue economy industries, ranging from offshore and marine energy, to fisheries management and maritime transport

items.title: Multiple Testing Of Composite Null Hypotheses With High Dimensional Count Data: A Local False Discovery Rate Approach
items.summary: High throughput sequencing technology is routinely used to generate high dimensional (HD) count data. One objective is to determine which variables are associated with a covariate via the testing of multiple null hypotheses, say $H_m:β_m = 0$ for $m = 1, 2, ..., M$ where each $β_m$ is a regression parameter. The standard approach computes a $p$-value for each null hypothesis and applies some false discovery rate (FDR) method to determine which null hypotheses are rejected, i.e. which variables can be discovered as associated with the covariate. However, even if data are ``well modeled'', this approach tends to provide a misleading list of discoveries in that some ``uninteresting'' negligible associations ($β_m \approx 0$) are discovered, while other interesting associations are not. This paper formally addresses this issue using Poisson Mixture models and a Local FDR (PMLFDR) procedure for testing of multiple composite null hypotheses $H_m:β_m\in[-ε,ε]$. It is shown that PMLFDR procedures allow for consistently estimable expressions for overdispersion, provide asymptotically optimal FDR control, and are robust with respect to model misspecification. Simulation studies and real data analysis illustrate that PMLFDR procedures perform favorably compared to established procedures in that they a) are flexible enough to model most HD count data regardless of the technology used in generation b) allow for continuous and categorical covariates and c) yield more meaningful discoveries without sacrificing FDR control.

items.title: Exact Online $Q_n$ Estimation: Exploiting Sliding-Window Rank Invariance
items.summary: The $Q_n$ scale estimator (Rousseeuw and Croux, 1993) combines a 50% finite-sample breakdown point with high Gaussian efficiency, but its computation requires selecting an order statistic among the $\binom{n}{2}$ pairwise distances. We study exact online $Q_n$ computation in a sliding window by exploiting temporal rank coherence between consecutive windows. Formalizing the multiset decomposition of surviving pairwise distances in terms of strict and weak rank counts, we derive a tie-exact dual-rank update that verifies whether the previous unscaled estimate remains valid in $\mathcal{O}(\log n)$ comparisons while maintaining the sorted window in $\mathcal{O}(n)$ time. When the target rank shifts by $m$ positions, a localized row-heap procedure initialized via a monotonic two-pointer frontier scan extracts the new exact order statistic in $\mathcal{O}(n + m\log n)$ comparisons without materializing the difference matrix, complemented by a hybrid fallback that executes frontier-guided implicit matrix selection in $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$ time for larger rank shifts. On deterministic multi-regime stress streams, our implementation matches the offline batch reference. In repeated same-platform benchmarks on a synthetic Gaussian stream, our implementation achieves median internal throughputs from 2,220,000 updates/s ($n=25$) and 1,140,000 updates/s ($n=51$) to 127,000 updates/s ($n=201$), outperforming both the exact FQN baseline ($2.5\times$ to $6.4\times$) and the approximate AFQN sketch ($1.3\times$ to $2.7\times$) across all tested window sizes.

items.title: Revisiting Generalized Median Estimators: Exact Bitwise Computation and Gray Code Acceleration
items.summary: Generalized median estimators evaluate the median of a symmetric kernel over all $M = \binom{n}{k}$ subsets of size $k$. Exhaustive evaluation was considered impractical even for $n = 29, k = 5$ ($M = 118,755$), prompting stochastic subsampling (Wilde and Grimshaw, 2013). We show that this barrier is computational, not combinatorial: storing all subsets requires $Θ(kM)$ space, whereas stateful enumeration uses $\mathcal{O}(k)$ auxiliary state and retains only $M$ kernel values. We combine two exhaustive traversals with three-way Quickselect and a deterministic median-of-medians fallback, giving worst-case $\mathcal{O}(M)$ selection. Gosper's successor takes $\mathcal{O}(k)$ kernel work per subset for $n < w$; a Revolving Door Gray code changes one element out and one in, enabling $\mathcal{O}(1)$ kernel updates between recalibrations and $\mathcal{O}(M + kM/P)$ total time. We derive floating-point error bounds for the location ($h_1$) and mean-centered sample variance ($h_2$) kernels and their resulting median. For $n = 29, k = 5$, our ANSI C implementation evaluates all $118,755$ subsets in $0.74$ ms and $0.71$ ms, respectively. A direct C sweep places the crossover with partial lexicographic unranking at approximately $18,000$-$23,000$ subsets ($15\%$-$19\%$ of $M$), below the $32,160$-$45,420$ subsets required by Wilde and Grimshaw's sequential approximation at $ε= 0.01$.

items.title: Hidden Semi-Markov Models for Fully Functional Time Series
items.summary: Functional time series have a wide range of practical applications to modeling complex datasets such as Electroencephalogram (EEG) and other biological signals. Often latent states are hidden within the data dictating how a system is behaving and changing over time. The Hidden Markov Model (HMM) is one common and highly applicable latent state space model where the hidden state sequence evolves as a Markov chain.
