The estimated effect on the probability of a diabetologist visit is 16.3 percentage points one semester after adoption and 39.3 percentage points four semesters after adoption, relative to a 55.2% visit probability in the semester before adoption. HbA1c testing and a broader process-of-care index show similar positive patterns, although the evidence is less precise. The visit estimates remain sensitive to the trend-extrapolation assumption and should therefore be interpreted conditionally on that restriction. The findings are consistent with a task-based view in which automation substitutes for routine dosing decisions while complementing clinical labor through interpretive, adjustment, and supervisory tasks. Patient-facing automation may therefore reorganize rather than simply reduce healthcare use.

items.title: Probabilistic Causal Panel Analysis
items.summary: Many causal panel estimators construct counterfactuals using weights or latent structure estimated directly from observed outcomes, making their estimates sensitive to observation noise. Bayesian hierarchical models can account for this noise and pool information across related observations. Existing Bayesian approaches to causal panel analysis, however, typically specify counterfactual imputation within the probabilistic model, so changing estimators may require a new formulation. We develop a framework that learns the latent untreated panel with a probabilistic model and applies established causal estimators to its posterior draws. The model accommodates non-Gaussian observations and structured pooling, while re-estimation across draws propagates uncertainty through counterfactual imputation. We establish conditions for posterior consistency and characterize how pooling affects imputation risk. Under correct posterior specification, we show that the excess Bayes risk of our approach is bounded by the causal estimator's expected squared imputation error when given the true latent outcomes in observed untreated cells. We also develop a fast cross-validation approach for model selection and calibration of predictive uncertainty for treatment effects. We use simulations to examine when pooling helps or harms imputation and cross-validation to assess whether probabilistic modeling improves accuracy in multiple empirical applications.

items.title: Robust Trust
items.summary: An agent chooses an action based on her private information and a recommendation from an informed but potentially misaligned adviser. With a known probability, the adviser truthfully reports his signal; with the remaining probability, he can send any message. We characterize robustly optimal decision rules that maximize the agent's worst-case expected payoff. Every optimal rule is equivalent to a trust-region policy in belief space: the adviser's reported beliefs are taken at face value if they fall within the trust region but are otherwise projected onto the trust region's boundary. We derive alignment thresholds above which advice is strictly valuable, explicitly characterize the solution in binary-state environments, and develop a procedure for computing the trust region numerically.

items.title: Unit-Level Conformal Inference for Panel Counterfactuals
items.summary: We develop conformal inference for panel counterfactual estimators using the exchangeability of prediction errors across units rather than over time. Existing conformal methods for panels with few treated units rely on temporal properties of treated-unit residuals, which are vulnerable to strong temporal heterogeneity such as nonstationarity. We instead hold out each control unit, hide its relevant outcomes, and predict them using the same rule applied to the treated unit. Target-date estimators, including difference-in-differences and synthetic control, use controls' pre-treatment and target-date outcomes to construct the counterfactual, allowing both full conformal confidence sets and Jackknife+ intervals. Full-path estimators, including factor-model imputation and matrix completion, also use controls' outcomes at other post-treatment dates; for these, we use the Jackknife+. Both procedures yield finite-sample, period-wise confidence sets under this across-unit exchangeability, without requiring stationarity or random assignment. We characterize when the coverage holds and show why a common prediction rule alone does not ensure it. For multiple treated units, a block Jackknife+ covers their average effect, while a relabeling test is exact for sharp nulls over all treated cells. We show that the synthetic control placebo test is a full conformal test of no effect that extends to full-path estimators. We also relate our procedures to a parametric bootstrap and classify common estimators by the inference they allow. We illustrate our procedures in three empirical applications.

items.title: Alternative Computational Formulations for Testing Discrete-Choice Random Utility Models: Half-Space and Network-Flow Formulations
items.summary: This paper develops computational algorithms for testing discrete-choice random utility models (RUM). The set of RUM-consistent choice probabilities forms a polytope, and existing computational methods rely on its vertex representation. We exploit alternative half-space (Block--Marschak inequalities) and network-flow representations to develop two methods based on the alternating direction method of multipliers and a flow-based column-generation algorithm. Compared with current vertex-based methods, our algorithms are better suited to GPU implementation. We establish convergence guarantees and provide optimality certificates for all three algorithms. The resulting algorithms achieve $100$--$600\times$ speedups over existing methods. The solver based on our methods is publicly available on Github at \href{https://github.com/mingxiz/d-rum-testing-gpu}{\texttt{d-rum-testing-gpu}}.

items.title: Identification and estimation for matrix time series CP-factor models
items.summary: We propose a new method for identifying and estimating the CP-factor models for matrix time series. Unlike the generalized eigenanalysis-based method of Chang et al. (2023) for which the convergence rates of the associated estimators may suffer from small eigengaps as the asymptotic theory is based on some matrix perturbation analysis, the proposed new method enjoys faster convergence rates which are free from any eigengaps. It achieves this by turning the problem into a joint diagonalization of several matrices whose elements are determined by a basis of a linear system, and by choosing the basis carefully to avoid near co-linearity (see Proposition 5 and Section 4.3). Furthermore, unlike the generalized eigenanalysis-based method which requires the two factor loading matrices to be full-ranked, the proposed new method can handle rank-deficient factor loading matrices. Illustration with both simulated and real matrix time series data shows the advantages of the proposed new method.

items.title: A General Theory of Dynamic Mechanism Design: Joint Optimization of Contracting, Information-Production Technology, and Disclosure
items.summary: We develop a general theory of dynamic mechanism design that jointly optimizes contracting, information-production technology, and disclosure across a broad class of economic environments with general allocation constraints. Hidden actions, endogenous information acquisition, learning, and disclosure interact through dynamic incentives. We accommodate correlated private information, interdependent preferences, and potentially infinite-dimensional allocations. We introduce joint perfect Bayesian equilibrium, establish the Dynamic Revelation Principle, and recursively characterize incentive compatibility. Under private values with informational interdependence, we characterize joint incentives through choice obedience, reporting-envelope first-order conditions, and global integral monotonicity. We derive an exact dynamic information-rent identity, dynamic revenue equivalence, and dynamic virtual surplus. Comparing first-best, two second-best, and third-best contracts distinguishes information rents, hidden-action implementation costs, and direct information-production expenditures, revealing nonadditive interactions of either sign and branched outcomes. Applications show Milgrom-Weber revenue-ranking reversal with endogenous acquisition, no efficient first-price equilibrium under Gaussian signals, and absent, interior, or full financial-contract disclosure.

items.title: Affirmative Action in India with Hierarchical Reservations
items.summary: We study the design of affirmative action mechanisms, focusing on India's system of horizontal reservations within vertical reservations. We consider a one-to-all policy, under which an applicant eligible for multiple horizontal categories simultaneously contributes toward each category's minimum guarantee. When horizontal reservations have a hierarchical structure, we introduce a choice rule that selects the unique merit-optimal set of applicants subject to these guaranties, satisfies the substitutes condition and size monotonicity. In a matching-with-contracts framework, we show that the generalized deferred acceptance mechanism is stable, strategy-proof, and eliminates justified envy under aggregate choice rules using the hierarchical choice rule in each vertical category. We establish a fundamental trade-off between merit and affirmative action between the one-to-all and one-to-one counting policies.

items.title: Predictive Uncertainty with Revised Economic Data
items.summary: Data revisions create uncertainty that outlives the first publication of an economic indicator. We develop a framework that turns an existing point forecast of the first release into a predictive distribution for a later release. The framework combines forecast-error records with official-release histories, including periods without recorded forecasts. We establish identification conditions and, from the component distributions, construct sharp bounds for directional probabilities and dependence-robust prediction intervals. We also show when additional revision records strictly improve estimation precision for a fixed rare-tail bound. Monte Carlo simulations quantify the predictive gains from longer release histories. Across four US inflation series, full histories improve interval scores relative to forecast-matched histories, with the largest gains in PCE. The conditional procedures lower pooled interval scores by 27--28 percent relative to a joint stochastic-volatility benchmark. With recency weighting, they match its observed coverage using intervals 34--36 percent narrower.

items.title: Aggregating Rankings of Coalitions to Rank Individuals
items.summary: We develop an ordinal framework for aggregating a profile of rankings of coalitional performances to determine the ranking of individuals. From university ratings to the assessment of team-sports players, we often evaluate individuals based on their coalitional performances. Although such evaluation has been addressed by cooperative game theory, it is only recently that its ordinal counterpart, social ranking theory (Moretti, 2015), has emerged. As most of the literature considers a single coalitional ranking (which corresponds to a real-valued characteristic function), we extend the model to allow a profile of coalitional rankings (which corresponds to a multidimensional characteristic function). We tackle the aggregation problem by introducing three families of inter-profile axioms, each representing how the rankings should interact or contribute to the output. After revealing fundamental impossibilities concerning the reconciliation of different families, we characterize a new solution, Pareto-extension Lex-cel (PEL), via some weaker versions of the inter-profile axioms. PEL extends Lex-cel, which is a central solution in social ranking theory, by analogy with Sen's Pareto extension rule. Our results develop the connection between classical Arrovian aggregation, cooperative game theory, and social ranking theory.

items.title: Hidden Eligibility and the Credibility of Adoption
items.summary: Subsidies encourage adoption, but they also change what others can learn from it. We study a government that chooses the amount and coverage of an early-adoption rebate and the information released about eligibility. Both early and late adoption create positive externalities. When eligibility is hidden, expanding the programme makes adoption less informative. As the benefit of early adoption rises, the optimal programme jumps from a small one that preserves imitation to a larger one that gives it up. We show that partial disclosure can support intermediate coverage and strictly improve on both optimally chosen opacity and full disclosure. An optimal report certifies the eligibility of some users, leaving the remaining adoptions sufficiently persuasive to induce imitation. We characterise the conditions for this policy and compare coverage under the alternative reporting rules. Analytical extensions allow delivery failures, private information, and heterogeneous adoption costs. The discontinuous change in optimal coverage can persist even when cost heterogeneity makes welfare continuous in coverage.

items.title: How optimistic inflow forecasts distort dispatch, prices, and contracts in hydro-dominated power systems: evidence from Brazil
items.summary: Centralized hydrothermal planning models determine generation schedules and electricity spot prices based on inflow forecasts in audited-cost power systems, such as those prevalent in Latin America, and provide operational benchmarks and decision support in hydro-dominated competitive electricity markets. Consequently, biased forecasts can propagate directly into both operational decisions and market outcomes. This paper studies how persistent optimistic inflow forecast bias can propagate through a hydrothermal power system, from system operation to market outcomes. For a stylized hydrothermal model, we show that optimistic bias weakly reduces water values and weakly increases first-stage hydro discharge relative to the unbiased optimum, thereby lowering reservoir storage and postponing thermal commitment. Using official Brazilian planning and operational data, we provide empirical evidence consistent with this mechanism. We then conduct controlled SDDP experiments to compare policies trained under biased and bias-corrected inflow-forecast processes, evaluating both under the same bias-corrected inflow scenarios. The policy based on biased forecasts produces lower reservoir levels, delayed dry-season thermal dispatch, sharper spot-price peaks, higher reliability risk, and higher expected operating costs. Finally, a stylized contracting exercise indicates that these distortions increase the price-quantity risk of a representative hydropower producer and reduce its willingness-to-contract. The results indicate that inflow-forecast bias can be a source of operational inefficiency, reliability risk, and distorted market incentives in hydro-dominated power systems. The insights and policy implications drawn in this paper may be relevant to hydro-dominated systems and electricity markets that are increasingly reliant on energy storage.

items.title: Resource Allocation with Midterm Review
items.summary: A principal funds an agent's project over two periods, with a midterm review providing a public signal about project quality. The agent privately knows the quality and always prefers more funding, while the principal wants to match funding to quality. We identify two reversal phenomena in the optimal mechanism. First, the principal's expected payoff is strictly higher in the first period than in the second, even though she is better informed after the review. Second, higher-quality projects receive more funding initially but less funding following a bad review, and may receive less funding following a good review as well.

items.title: When AI Improves Answers but Slows Knowledge Creation: Matching and Dynamic Knowledge Creation in Digital Public Goods
items.summary: Generative AI helps users solve problems more efficiently, but can also replace exchanges between people with private conversations with chatbots. When more problems are solved privately, fewer problem-solving episodes are converted into reusable public knowledge for others. We build a dynamic model of public good provision where agents post and answer questions on a public platform. AI can shrink the platform's archive through two margins. Private diversion can reduce the posted volume of knowledge-enhancing questions (the flow margin), while contributor exit can lower conditional resolution (the resolution margin). Low-archive traps can arise with or without AI, because a thin archive makes public answering too costly to sustain; AI can narrow the viable region. The model gives conditional empirical predictions that distinguish demand-side diversion from supply-side pool thinning under explicit identifying restrictions. Logging private solutions adds archive inflow, while rewards for answering strengthen contribution incentives.

items.title: The opposing informational effects of AI trading
items.summary: Better artificial intelligence (AI) can improve individual forecasts without making prices better at revealing new information. In a competitive market with resource-constrained forecasting, more capable algorithms can substitute analysis of public records for private observations, reducing the private information aggregated into prices. The same trades can convey sophisticated public-data analysis to investors unable to perform it themselves. We establish conditions under which these effects coexist and the private benefit of further computation falls. Numerical equilibrium calculations and finite-data neural-market experiments exhibit corresponding patterns. Out-of-sample earnings forecasts and controlled language-model tasks show related patterns of information substitution. In the neural experiment, wider adoption increases the predictive value of price for limited observers, reduces it for advanced observers, and lowers the benefit of upgrading by 44\%. Retraining by investors who did not upgrade can amplify the loss of private-information precision. The informational consequences of AI trading depend on what prices reveal and who can use them.

items.title: Local Asymptotic Power of Honest Confidence Intervals
items.summary: Honest or bias-aware confidence intervals, conservative against untestable bias, are now standard in DiD, IV, RD, and factor models. This paper characterises the local power of their tests, which has three regimes set by the bias bound's rate relative to the sampling rate. A bound vanishing faster than the standard error costs nothing, one of the same order costs a bounded amount, and a dominating bound, typical at the parametric rate, leaves zero local power. This loss is intrinsic to honesty, and the standard bias-aware interval is rate-optimal. The paper recommends reporting the power ``dead zone'' half-width alongside bias-aware intervals.

items.title: Disenfranchisement in Spatial Voting Games
items.summary: The questions of voting rights, group membership, and the boundaries of acceptable discourse all involve a recursive, self-stability issue, wherein the voters, group members, and acceptable commentators are often the ultimate arbiters of their own rules for inclusion and exclusion. In order to understand how ideological or issue diversity may impact the stability of such inclusion and exclusion, we introduce franchise elections, where voting members of a group vote to change the electorate. In particular, when agents are positioned inside an ideological or issue space, a social choice function that aggregates agent viewpoints induces a preference for agents over group composition, where agents prefer groups that improve the social choice function outcome for them. We demonstrate that when ideological space is two-dimensional, these franchise elections can generate complex behavior and that this complexity exists for any social choice function. Using the Yolk social choice function from voting theory, we illustrate that franchise elections can predict that agents attempting to introduce a new ideological axis perpendicular to an existing left-right spectrum risk disenfranchisement unless they ally with either side of the spectrum, and that franchise elections can cycle with any period.

items.title: Constrained Stochastic Policy Targeting under Heterogeneous Partial Interference
items.summary: Under heterogeneous interference, treating individuals with particular characteristics affects the population average outcome through their heterogeneous direct response to treatment and indirect effect on others, creating opportunities for efficient policy design. For instance, policymakers may minimize resource use by vaccinating individuals identified as superspreaders to achieve a target reduction in disease incidence. In such setting, we first study the problem of learning individualized stochastic treatment policies that minimize population average treatment probability subject to a prespecified outcome target. We propose an estimation approach based on a smooth surrogate for constraint violations and interference-aware inverse-probability-weighting or self-normalized estimators of the population average outcome, and establish finite-sample regret guarantees for both estimators. We also consider the complementary problem of maximizing the population average outcome subject to a constraint on average treatment probability. We apply the proposed methodology to a Colombian conditional cash transfer program aimed at improving school attendance. The application demonstrates that accounting for interference and individualizing treatment probabilities can reduce resource use relative to policies that ignore interference or impose homogeneous treatment probabilities.

items.title: Making Experiment Results Comparable through Sitewide Impact Estimation
items.summary: Roblox spans many product surfaces-discovery, the virtual economy, creator tools-that differ sharply in reach and in how much the affected population contributes to any sitewide metric. A randomized experiment shows whether a treatment works for the users in its sample, but this experiment lift is not comparable across surfaces, because surfaces differ in reach and in their contribution to sitewide metrics. The quantity a strategic decision needs is a counterfactual-how much an aggregated sitewide metric (e.g., total platform play time) would move if the treatment reached 100% of its target population, which may be only part of the sitewide population, during the measurement period. We call this sitewide impact. Its scaling factor, which we call the coverage factor, combines the reach and the target population's contribution to the sitewide metric under no treatment. Hence a low-reach surface whose users carry much of the metric could outrank a high-reach surface whose users carry little. We develop two estimators under this framing: one for difference-in-means metrics and one for variant-level ratio metrics (a metric defined as a ratio of two population aggregates). Empirically, experiment lift is a poor proxy for sitewide impact-across 139 experiments that are statistically significant on time spent, the Spearman rank correlation between the two is 0.20, and 5 of the 10 largest experiment lifts are among the 10 largest sitewide impacts. We validate the estimator with A/A tests and against a long-term holdout, and apply it to cross-domain prioritization and attributing year-over-year growth to shipped innovations.

items.title: Match classification in the last round of four-team round-robin tournaments
items.summary: Classification of matches played in the last rounds of sports competitions is a well-established tool for evaluating tournament designs. Our paper offers the first comparison of deterministic and probabilistic match classification models by analysing the most prominent example of four-team round-robin competitions, the group stage of the FIFA World Cup. We show that both models are highly relevant in practice: all (four) deterministic and (six) probabilistic match types occurred in the 2014 and 2018 FIFA World Cups, respectively. The probabilistic model, which accounts for the relative benefits of attacking and defending, provides a deeper insight; for instance, the competitive matches from the deterministic approach can be of any of the six probabilistic types. Therefore, the probabilistic model is used to decompose the impact of three reforms introduced in the 2026 FIFA World Cup: the expansion to 48 teams, the modified qualification rules, and head-to-head tie-breakers.

items.title: Social Media Can Suppress or Fuel Misinformation at Its Source, Depending on Civic Engagement
items.summary: Social media is widely viewed as a channel for spreading misinformation, but its effects may begin earlier, by shaping whether misinformation is produced in the first place. We examine whether social media suppresses or amplifies the supply of misinformation and identify civic engagement as a key boundary condition. Using data on the GDP reporting of Chinese local governments from 2011 to 2019, we find that social media adoption reduces GDP misreporting only when civic engagement is high. This reduction is driven by posts that disclose specific economic data rather than promotional content. When civic engagement is low, however, social media adoption instead increases GDP misreporting. These findings reveal a dual upstream role of social media in the misinformation process: it can deter misinformation at its source when disclosures are exposed to engaged citizens, but can amplify its supply when civic engagement is limited.

items.title: Learning Dynamics of the Influencer's Game in Resource Landscapes
items.summary: Across domains as varied as ecology, economics, and online platforms, individuals are incentivized to position themselves within resource-rich strategy spaces. In this work we introduce a new spatial game framework called the influencer's game. Within this new framework players' strategies are represented as positions within a trait space. Players then receive a share of a portion of a resource based on their relative influence at that resource's points traits. For the influencer's game, we show that there is a unique symmetric Nash equilibrium that exists under strict log-concavity of the influence kernel. Using the unique equilibrium we show that the stability of the system depends on the influence kernel's parameters, number of players, and the resource distribution shape. For any dimension we demonstrate a stability threshold that depends on both the scatter and curvature of the players. When this threshold is crossed, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes and gives way to a variety of bifurcation types; including, specialist clusters, limit cycles, and sub-games that reproduce the larger game's structure. We ground these results using real-world data for resources as a demonstration of the game's application. Finally we extend the game dynamics to use multi-agent reinforcement learning and further show that the predicted bifurcation structure persists under partial observability and discretized strategy spaces. In all, the influencer's game provides a novel framework for predicting when competitive pressure drives convergence versus fragmentation with possible applications across domains.

items.title: Exploitation, class income and welfare in a Sraffian economy with consumption preferences
items.summary: This paper develops a Sraffian model of simple reproduction in which production prices and functional income distribution remain classically determined, while class consumption is chosen optimally at those prices and incomes. it then shows that once workers and capitalists choose consumption bundles according to class-specific preferences, rather than consuming fixed baskets, surplus value, exploitation rates, total profits, and capitalist welfare need not rise monotonically with the profit rate. The framework defines distributive Engel curves, tracing how consumption, profits, labor exploitation, and welfare vary along the wage-profit frontier. Higher profitability may expand capitalists' nominal claim on surplus, yet alter relative prices in ways that reduce their real consumption and welfare. The result qualifies standard Marxian and Sraffian accounts of net product distribution based on the wage-profit curve.

items.title: Who sees the sea? Sea-view potential by façade and floor from cadastral LoD1 models on the Costa del Sol
items.summary: Views are among the most valued and least measured attributes of a home. We present an open-data method that estimates the sea-view potential of every free façade of every residential building at three floors (ground, middle and top; other floors take the nearest of them), from cadastral footprints with floor counts and a national terrain model. Run for 158,060 buildings of 21 municipalities on Spain's Costa del Sol in under an hour on two cores, it finds that 52 % of buildings see some sea from their top floor and 36 % have an open view (20° or more). Traced over a LiDAR surface in a pilot, scores agree with the model's inside cadastral footprints (96.7 % of viewpoints in the same class at 20°), but structures the cadastre does not record lower the sea seen from the top floor by 6.1--9.0° on average. Against the photographs of 93 homes for sale, labelled blind by AI models of two developers with ties decided by the author, the score has an AUC of 0.80 (95 % CI 0.70--0.89; 0.81 against the first-round labels); at 20° it is sensitive (0.90) but not specific (0.45). Dwelling figures depend on how dwellings are allocated to façades and floors: 42 % of dwellings are on a floor with open-view potential under the main rule, and 12--45 % across the allocation, geometry and vegetation scenarios tested. As an application, higher-income census sections tend to have more modelled view potential within municipalities, with uncertain size and fragile inference (about two effective clusters); on terrain alone the difference largely disappears. Code and façade-level data reproduce the main results.

items.title: Tolerable Inflation, Intolerable Uncertainty
items.summary: How much of an inflation deviation a central bank should tolerate is a well-defined optimum in the New Keynesian model, but it cannot be identified: optimal accommodation of supply shocks and an unwarranted drift of the effective inflation target are observationally equivalent. This impossibility has a cost. A public that cannot verify the bank's intention prices each expected point of overshoot, so uncertainty about inflation is flat below the announced target and rises linearly above it: the observational-equivalence effect. Professional forecasts, swap and option markets and realized inflation all show this pattern, with the kink at the announced number. A second and larger effect produces the same shape: inflation is more volatile when it is high, and in realized inflation that level effect is mostly energy. Both effects load on the distance from the target, so the data admit the observational-equivalence effect without isolating it, and its cost cannot be estimated with the data at hand. We therefore cannot say how optimal monetary policy should change on its account, but three policy conclusions survive: in the textbook model, not observing the slope of the Phillips curve and the composition of shocks never calls for tolerating less; the announced target remains worth having, because it compresses beliefs at the target; and the central bank can monitor the point-years inflation spends above target, on which the effect is charged, and read inflation uncertainty net of the distance from the target. Normalized Uncertainty provides that reading. In French loan-level data, raw inflation uncertainty is unrelated to corporate loan rates after controls, whereas a one-standard-deviation increase in Normalized Uncertainty is associated with rates 89 basis points higher. The correction also reveals a negative association with growth across countries and alters euro-area time-series results.

items.title: Safe manipulation of tops-only voting rules
items.summary: We study tops-only voting rules on the domain of all preferences with a unique top, focusing on manipulation by risk-avoiding voters. Following Hartman et al.(2025), we measure resistance to manipulation by the RAT-degree: the minimum number of other voters' reports that a voter needs to observe for a ``safe'' manipulation to become possible. Given the observed reports, such a manipulation weakly improves on truthful reporting under every completion of the unobserved reports and strictly improves on it under at least one completion. For any finite set of at least three alternatives, we show that anonymity, unanimity, and winner monotonicity imply an upper bound of $\lceil n/2\rceil$ on the RAT-degree, where $n$ is the number of voters. We provide exact characterizations of the RAT-degree for anonymous generalized median voter schemes and voting by quotas, without imposing single-peakedness or separability on preferences. For odd $n$, the median voter rule and objectwise majority rule uniquely maximize the RAT-degree within their respective classes and attain the general upper bound.

items.title: Sensitivity Analysis for Linear Estimators
items.summary: We propose a framework for building sensitivity analyses for linear estimators. We measure the degree of identification failure by the change of measure between the observed distribution and a hypothetical target distribution under which a standard estimator would identify the parameter of interest. Under L_infinity bounds on that derivative, the identified set has closed-form sharp bounds that require no numerical optimization and that are computable and continuous when the derivative is unbounded, nesting Manski-type worst-case bounds and existing characterizations that require bounded changes of measure. The framework nests several selection models for average potential outcomes, yielding the established worst-case bounds of each design. The framework yields a new model family for regression discontinuity (RD) that delivers the first sensitivity analysis on the conditional average treatment effect under manipulation. We show that a bootstrap procedure yields valid confidence intervals. An empirical application shows that a modest restriction on manipulation delivers bounds far more informative than worst-case bounds.

items.title: Bridging Distant Ideas: the Impact of AI on R&D and Recombinant Innovation
items.summary: We study how artificial intelligence (AI) affects firms' incentives to pursue incremental versus radical knowledge recombinations. We develop a model of recombinant innovation embedded in a Schumpeterian quality-ladder framework, in which innovation arises from recombining ideas across varying distances in a knowledge space. R&D consists of multiple tasks, a fraction of which can be performed by AI. AI facilitates access to distant knowledge domains, but at the same time it also increases the aggregate rate of creative destruction, shortening the monopoly duration that rewards radical innovations. We obtain three main results. First, the effect of increasing the share of AI-automated R&D tasks is non-monotonic under specific conditions: firms initially target more radical innovations, but beyond a threshold they shift the focus toward incremental innovations. Second, with falling optimal distance, we may have increasing expected log-growth of knowledge due to higher innovation frequency or a hump-shaped growth. Finally, we identify a sufficient condition under which the target distance chosen in the decentralized equilibrium is sub-optimal from a social welfare point of view.

items.title: Broken Adaptive Ridge in High-Dimensional Vector Autoregressions
items.summary: We study regularized estimation in high-dimensional vector autoregressions under physical dependence and row-wise approximate sparsity using the Broken Adaptive Ridge (BAR) estimator. BAR is an iteratively reweighted Ridge procedure whose fixed-point first-order conditions imply a coordinatewise thresholding rule that produces exact zeros. We show that the BAR estimation error can be analyzed on the union of the population support above the BAR threshold and the support selected in the sample. The size of this union can be controlled at the rate implied by approximate sparsity, allowing us to establish the required restricted-curvature condition and derive L1, L2, and prediction error rates when the number of regressors grows polynomially with the sample size and may exceed it. Under exact sparsity, the resulting rates recover the familiar rates for sparse high-dimensional estimation. Monte Carlo experiments across a range of high-dimensional VAR designs show that BAR delivers strong estimation and forecasting performance, and retains a high share of relevant coefficients relative to Lasso, adaptive Lasso, and SCAD. An application to U.S. inflation forecasting using FRED-MD shows particularly strong performance at the one-month horizon.

items.title: Linear Multidimensional Regression with Interactive Fixed-Effects
items.summary: This paper studies a linear model for multidimensional panel data of three or more dimensions with unobserved interactive fixed-effects. The main estimator is a weighted-within transformation, which is Neyman orthogonal and requires one preliminary step. In that step, the model is embedded within a two-dimensional panel framework where factor model methods in Bai (2009) lead to consistent, but slowly converging, estimates that serve as proxies for the fixed-effects. The weighted-within transformation is robust to multidimensional interactive fixed-effects and achieves the parametric rate of consistency. The estimator is shown to be asymptotically normal. The methods are implemented to estimate the demand elasticity for beer.

items.title: Positive Weights Do Not Certify TWFE Inference: A Design Diagnostic under Treatment-Effect Heterogeneity
items.summary: Conventional two-way fixed-effects (TWFE) inference need not be uniformly adequate even when all treatment weights are positive. Under a local treatment-effect drift, the statistic for the equally weighted treated-cell effect has worst-case mean shift $(c/q)Γ$, where $Γ=\sqrt{N_1}\|w-u\|_2$ is design-only and $q$ is the cluster-score noise scale. Projection matches the exposure to cohort, event-time, additive, and saturated group-time pilots; when residualized treatment is constant within treated group-time cells, $Γ_{\mathrm{gt}}=Γ$. A direct score estimator is feasible with fixed panel length as clusters grow. Because a debiased quadratic pilot is nonregular at zero, we use two regular one-sided procedures: a reverse-triangle multiplier lower bound to detect unsafe envelopes and covariance-aware noncentral-$χ^2$ inversion to certify adequacy. At $5\%$ nominal size with a five-point tolerance, the shift threshold is $0.652$. In the Callaway--Sant'Anna minimum-wage panel, where every treated-cell weight is positive, the saturated $95\%$ lower shift bound is $0.793$, so conventional inference is not uniformly certified. A complementary Brazilian property-tax reanalysis with $2{,}840$ municipalities withholds certification in all four classes; its smallest lower bound is $1.040$. Under the maintained many-cluster approximation, castle-doctrine homicide passes for additive cohort-plus-event-time heterogeneity with a $95\%$ upper bound of $0.236$; its saturated covariance lacks one required rank. Divorce is inconclusive. These envelopes are not predictions of realized rejection. The diagnostic separates point correction, uniform exposure, and statistically warranted certification.

items.title: Huge If True: Learning from the Size of the Surprise
items.summary: Responses to earnings surprises depend on an unknown multiplier mapping earnings to value. Investors, however, learn about the news and the multiplier from the same number. Large surprises may indicate small multipliers and tiny surprises large ones. We model how greater uncertainty about the multiplier attenuates responses on average but makes them steeper near zero surprises. In an incentivized experiment, we find that greater processing constraints lower average sensitivity but raise it near zero. We confirm this with real-world earnings announcements: stocks with higher valuation uncertainty, our proxy for multiplier uncertainty, respond less on average but more steeply near zero.

items.title: Endogenous Parcel Contiguity and Rent Indeterminacy in a Finite-Household Monocentric City
items.summary: We study a monocentric city with finitely many households, each of which may hold any measurable set of land and incurs commuting costs that depend on the spatial distribution of its holdings. In equilibrium, every parcel is an interval and parcels are ordered by lot size from the center outward. The freedom to adjust land holdings at any location restricts supporting rents to a band between the competing bid rents and the assigned household's bid rent. This band excludes rents that support the same allocation when lots are restricted to intervals, including the one constructed by Berliant and Fujita (1992), and makes the existence of a supporting rent a substantive question even with identical households. We give sufficient conditions for the existence of a locally supporting rent that meets every household's budget and deters all small deviations. We also show that any equilibrium minimizes the real resource cost of attaining equilibrium utilities and extend the sorting result to heterogeneous households under a single-crossing condition. Finally, we discuss the relation to hedonic models, distinguishing the prices of whole parcels from location-specific rents that govern the cost of changes in parcel boundaries and fragmentation.

items.title: Menu Design Meets Market Design: Strategic Simplicity vs. Choice Complexity
items.summary: Strategic simplicity removes the incentive to misreport preferences, but it does not ensure that participants can identify what they prefer. We study this distinction in a laboratory experiment on serial dictatorships, where optimal play only requires choosing one's favorite bundle of real-effort tasks. Participants make fifteen incentivized choices among bundles that vary in how many tasks they combine. They choose either from a large menu or through a series of binary choices. Having made all choices, they unexpectedly reconsider each assignment against a previously rejected alternative. We find that roughly one in six choices is reversed and almost one in five involves an objectively dominated bundle. Simplifying the choice architecture does not help. Binary decomposition even raises reversal rates among low-ability participants and further inflates their confidence about their choices.

items.title: Who Is Prioritized? Current Need versus Predicted Gains in China's Dibao Allocation: Evidence from a Revealed-Allocation Model
items.summary: Using the 2017--2021 China Household Finance Survey panel and a sample of 3,102 households that did not receive Dibao in 2017, this paper applies the BBK revealed-allocation model to examine how household economic circumstances and predicted policy gains explain observed Dibao receipt in China. We find that household income is the allocation criterion most difficult to substitute with other factors. When all gain-adjustment terms are positive, constraining the income-rank coefficient to be nonnegative reduces the model's original improvement in fit by approximately 33.6\%; by contrast, setting both predicted-gain coefficients for food consumption and education spending to zero still preserves approximately 95.6\% of that improvement. These results indicate that observed Dibao allocation places greater emphasis on prioritizing households facing current livelihood hardship than on pursuing predictable short-run improvements in expenditure outcomes. This allocation orientation reflects the trade-off in social assistance between basic-livelihood protection and expected policy gains and offers a new perspective on the potential long-run social-welfare value of basic-livelihood protection.

items.title: Social Networks and the Propagation of Household Shocks to Asset Prices
items.summary: When can local household disturbances move credit prices? I develop a financially weighted propagation operator on the social network. In a conditional household-intermediary equilibrium, its projection determines the household-demand component of the excess bond premium. Because responses decay at different rates across network patterns and channels, a location's relative financial importance generically changes with the horizon, so no single centrality measure summarizes exposure across horizons. Household measurements recover this projection exactly when they span independently measured demand sensitivities. Empirically, social exposure to storm-damaged counties is negatively associated with spending weeks later in counties outside the recorded footprints. In simulations on the observed network under the model's diffusion law, the operator predicts the propagated credit-premium component of held-out storms with about 30 percent less error than direct social exposure.

items.title: Intentionally Overidentifying Local Projections
items.summary: Local projections (LPs) have become a standard tool for estimating dynamic effects in macroeconomics and are typically implemented using ordinary least squares (OLS) for a given lag order. We propose an alternative approach that exploits additional lags as excluded instrumental variables (IVs). Under a finite-order model with martingale-difference shocks, the resulting (optimally weighted) IV estimator is never asymptotically less efficient than OLS and, as we show, can deliver substantial efficiency gains when data are persistent. For the unit-root AR(1) data with i.i.d. errors, our baseline IV estimator (with one overidentifying restriction) has asymptotic variance $2-h^{-1}$, compared with $h$, the asymptotic variance of the OLS lag-augmented estimator in Montiel Olea and Plagborg-Møller (2021), for an integer propagation horizon $h$. We then develop IV-based LP inference that is robust to unknown persistence and moderate local model misspecification. We also characterize the trade-off between the degree of misspecification and the number of additional lag controls. Through simulations and an empirical application, we demonstrate that the proposed method can yield meaningfully shorter confidence intervals for impulse responses than OLS in finite samples.

items.title: Designing Information in a Forest: Algorithmic Aspects
items.summary: The Bayesian persuasion framework models strategic information revelation by a sender to one or more receivers. We study an intricate version of the multi-receiver persuasion setting in which the communication hierarchy is a forest - i.e., some receivers observe more informative signals than others, and the partial ordering of the receivers according to the information they get is represented by a pre-specified directed forest. This model naturally captures interactions in hierarchical organizations, and it lies in between the two most commonly studied versions of Bayesian persuasion: private persuasion and public persuasion. Inspired by the classic model of private persuasion, we focus on a setting with a binary state of nature and binary-action heterogeneous receivers s.t. the sender's utility is a monotone function of the set of receivers taking a specific desirable action. We extend the computational tractability result for symmetric sender's utility from private persuasion to the forest hierarchy framework using methodology inspired by optimal transport theory. We further provide a polynomial-time algorithm when the sender's utility is modular. On the negative side, we show that, unlike in private persuasion, the case of a supermodular sender's utility function leads to an NP-hard optimization problem which further does not admit an FPTAS unless P=NP; this result holds even when each tree component of the forest is a chain of 3 receivers. To complement the hardness result, we provide a simple approximation algorithm with the approximation ratio depending linearly on the depth of the forest hierarchy. We further provide an analogous algorithm for the submodular utility case. Finally, beyond forest communication hierarchies, we rule out an FPTAS for the sender's optimal utility even in the symmetric utility case, unless P=NP.

items.title: Coal Mining, Women's Work, and Local Demographic Change: Evidence from Interwar Japan
items.summary: This paper examines how coal mining shaped local demographic change in interwar Japan, focusing on the role of women's work. Coal mines initially employed married couples as underground teams, offering women wages well above those in textile mills. The mechanization of haulage and the subsequent revision of labor regulations, enforced in 1933, removed most women from the pits. Linking mine locations with municipal-level census and vital statistics, I find that coal mining substantially increased local populations, mainly through the inflow of workers, whereas marriage and fertility rates in mining areas were lower than in surrounding areas. After women were removed from the pits, these gaps narrowed. Early-life mortality was higher in mining areas and increased with the number of female miners, consistent with occupational hazards to pregnant women, whereas there is little evidence of pollution channels.

items.title: Truthful compromise and insurance on a sphere
items.summary: Can public choice without transfers insure conflicting interests when action intensity is fixed? We require truthful reporting for every increasing-concave evaluation of alignment with private ideals. On a sphere, efficiency at profiles with at most three ideal directions forces fixed-weight random dictatorship; weaker tests suffice in two and three dimensions. From four dimensions, binary efficiency permits committees to insure members by placing outcome risk orthogonally to their reports. We identify restrictions shared by all mechanisms with these incentives and binary efficiency: binary winning probabilities determine mean outcomes at every profile and individual alignment distributions at planar three-camp profiles. When these probabilities depend only on camp size, complete insurance at balanced equilateral disagreement requires dimension proportional to population. In contrast, committees reduce each participant's welfare loss relative to certain zero alignment to any prescribed positive fraction of the equal-weight random-dictatorship loss in a population-independent dimension.

items.title: Random Utility Models in the Consumption-Budget Setting: Vertex and Network-Flow Characterizations
items.summary: This note supplements our paper \textit{Alternative Computational Formulations for Testing Discrete-Choice Random Utility Models: Half-Space and Network-Flow Formulations} and serves two purposes: 1. We clarify the conceptual distinctions between two classes of random utility models (RUM): those in the consumption-budget setting \citep{kitamura2019nonparametric} (hereafter KS) and those in the finite-alternative setting (e.g., Chapter~7 of \cite{chambers2016revealed}). In particular, we show (Theorem 1) that each rational type, as defined in KS, can be obtained as a coordinate projection of the deterministic choice vector induced by a strict preference ranking that satisfies what we call a patch-monotonicity condition. 2. We generalize the network-flow characterization for finite-alternative RUM in \cite{fiorini2004short} to the consumption-budget setting (Theorem 2). Specifically, we show that a vector of choice probabilities in the consumption-budget setting is rationalizable in the KS sense if and only if it is the image of a unit flow on a multi-arc powerset digraph under a fixed linear map. The key distinction is that our digraph allows multiple arcs between the same pair of nodes, whereas the digraph in Fiorini has at most one arc between any pair of nodes.

items.title: Post-Selection Inference for Partially Identified Parameters
items.summary: Partial identification of parameters such as average treatment effects, average partial effects and welfare is particularly common when using observational data and experimental data with imperfect compliance due to the endogeneity of individuals' treatment uptake. In this setting, the researcher is typically interested in a treatment or policy that is either selected from the estimated set of best-performers or arises from a data-dependent selection rule. In this paper, we develop new inference tools for partially-identified parameters chosen via these forms of selection. We develop three types of confidence intervals for data-dependent and partially-identified parameters, discuss how they apply to several examples of interest and prove their uniform asymptotic validity under weak assumptions.

items.title: Benefits and Costs of Adaptive Sampling
items.summary: Multi-armed bandits are widely used for sequential experimentation in clinical trials, public policy treatment, recommendation systems, and online platforms. While regret minimization and valid inference from adaptively collected data have each been studied individually, one question remains: when does adaptivity \emph{improve estimation precision} relative to uniform designs, and how should inference be balanced against the online cost of experimentation? We first study arm-level mean estimation under mean-squared-error (MSE) objectives. We characterize when an adaptive Neyman allocation, which allocates samples according to arm variance, yields strict MSE improvements over uniform sampling in finite samples. When there is variance heterogeneity across arms, these improvements arise at modest sample sizes, clarifying that adaptivity can be preferable for inference not only asymptotically, but also in finite-sample settings. We then study a joint inference--regret objective that accounts for the cost of assigning units to inferior arms during experimentation. We propose three policies: the Plug-in Oracle Rate Policy, Static-Allocation Rate Policy, and Neyman-Adaptive Rate Policy, all of which attain the oracle-optimal asymptotic rate. The latter two offer computationally efficient and easy-to-implement alternatives by combining existing regret-minimizing algorithms with inference-oriented sampling through closed-form mixing rules, avoiding repeated numerical optimization while being managerially interpretable. We compare their finite-sample statistical performance through simulations and empirically calibrated applications. The results highlight the relative strengths of our policies across instances and their tradeoffs between joint inference--regret performance and computational cost.

items.title: Approximating an Ideal Experiment with Induced Order Statistics
items.summary: Many economic questions concern the conditional distribution of an outcome at a fixed covariate value. We refer to observing i.i.d.\ draws from this distribution as an \emph{ideal experiment}, under which many statistical procedures admit exact, finite-sample guarantees. When the covariate is continuously distributed, however, this ideal experiment is unavailable. We provide a general method for approximating this ideal experiment using \emph{induced order statistics}, the outcomes attached to the nearest observed covariates. We derive explicit bounds on the approximation error in Hellinger and total variation distances. These bounds quantify how local approximation errors accumulate as the nearest-neighbor sample grows and provide a unified way to transfer rejection and coverage guarantees across statistical procedures. Under quadratic mean differentiability and local regularity of the covariate distribution, the bounds apply to both interior and boundary conditioning points and give explicit conditions on the growth of the nearest-neighbor sample. We illustrate the approach in four distinct applications: covariate balance testing in regression discontinuity designs, conditional quantile inference, conformal prediction at a fixed covariate value, and policy-irrelevance testing under network interference.

items.title: Orthogonal Scores and Double/Debiased Machine Learning for Possibly Misspecified GMM
items.summary: We develop Neyman orthogonal scores for GMM models that remain valid when the moment conditions may fail to hold. Existing score constructions typically require the moment conditions to hold exactly, which may fail in over-identified models, where the number of moment functions exceeds the number of parameters. We construct \emph{misspecification-robust} orthogonal score that has a closed form; it is the conventional orthogonal score plus adjustment terms, for the estimation of the Jacobian and of the weighting matrix, which are proportional to the population moment and vanish under correct specification. The moment functions may depend on nonparametric or machine learning first steps, and we show that double/debiased machine learning (DML) combined with the proposed scores and cross-fitting provides uniformly valid inference for a low-dimensional GMM estimand, while the conventional DML standard errors are inconsistent when the moment conditions fail. We illustrate the results in the partially linear instrumental variables (PLIV) model and in the local average treatment effects (LATE) model with multiple instruments.

items.title: AI and the Two Margins of Work: Why Job Losses Show Up Before Job Creation
items.summary: Technological change acts on labor demand at two margins: adjustment within established activities and the creation of additional activities, often by new firms. Payroll statistics record the first promptly and the second late. In the computing era, firms that entered in 1978 or later held 42 percent of payroll by 1998 and entering cohorts kept about 80 percent of their payroll after five years; in the industries most exposed to automation, incumbents contracted before entrants accumulated, a sequence that is precise early in the period and suggestive by its end. We develop a model in which one AI capability lowers the full cost of acceptable output in existing production and makes additional projects worth attempting, with founder effort separate from hired hours. If operating products re-scale instantly, automation displaces no aggregate hours; if they take time, hours fall first and recover as incumbents re-expand and new products arrive, with the long-run sign set by income effects. Establishment job flows through the first quarter of 2026 show no gradient on language-model exposure on either margin, which is what the model predicts under the observed adoption path and also what no effect on payroll would look like; studies with founding-task exposure find entry rising 10 to 20 percent. We propose a net reinstatement ratio and show that statistics which record new work late overstate displacement for years.

items.title: Dynamic Pooling and Regional Participation in Deceased-Donor Organ Allocation
items.summary: Moving from geographically fragmented to pooled waiting lists in deceased-donor organ transplantation can improve efficiency, but it raises concerns about regional fairness and participation incentives. This paper studies Pareto gains from such transitions in a multiclass queueing model with impatient agents, perishable items, and a tractable homogeneous compatibility friction. In contrast to standard approaches that emphasize static match quality or overlook regional incentives in dynamic contexts, this analysis identifies dynamic risk pooling as the primary source of Pareto improvements for regions. Pooling reduces organ waste resulting from stochastic supply-demand fluctuations, temporal mismatches, and random compatibility outcomes. Although this dynamic surplus theoretically enables Pareto improvements, a purely utilitarian policy that treats all patients equally across regions often fails to achieve these improvements when regions are asymmetric. In these situations, utilitarian redistribution removes an excessive number of organs from high-supply regions and violates their participation constraints. To address this conflict, it is demonstrated that the set of achievable utilities can be represented by mixtures of static priority index policies. Building on this structure, the Constrained Pareto Frontier Search (CPFS) is proposed as a polynomial-time procedure that computes an approximately optimal allocation policy with arbitrarily small participation-constraint violations, implemented as a single priority list with a lottery at registration. The results indicate that, by adjusting priority indices to ensure redistribution remains within the gains from pooled supply, demand, and compatibility risk, policymakers can achieve global efficiency while maintaining local participation incentives.

items.title: Setting Optimal Reserve Prices using Fine-Tuned Language Models
items.summary: Online auction houses must set reserve prices for highly differentiated products whose unstructured descriptions contain valuable demand information. Existing approaches generally require managers to specify product attributes in advance. We ask whether a language model can instead learn from listing descriptions and historical bids to set item-specific reserve prices before bidding begins. We fine-tune a pretrained text embedding language model using the structural likelihood of auction bids as its training objective. This directs representation learning toward the valuation distribution that determines the reserve decision. We show that consecutive upper bids identify the tail information needed to set an optimal reserve without observing or modeling the number of potential bidders. A split-sample estimator learns the representation on one half of the data and conducts structural estimation and inference conditional on that representation on the other. We apply the method to approximately 65,800 online used-vehicle auctions. With seller values calibrated to match the sale rate among listings, the model implies a counterfactual net increase of $165.8 million, representing a 14.6% increase above the incumbent reserve policy. The framework translates a listing description and a seller's value into an item-specific reserve recommendation without constructing a product taxonomy or requiring a bid history for the item being priced. It provides an approach to adapting language models for operational decisions in marketplaces where products are heterogeneous and demand-relevant information is recorded in text.

items.title: Model Selection for Off-Policy Evaluation via Bellman Tournaments
items.summary: Model selection and hyperparameter tuning pose a central challenge in off-policy evaluation (OPE) because estimation errors in fitted $Q$-functions and occupancy ratios cannot be directly evaluated using held-out transition data. Existing Bellman-residual-based validation methods often require auxiliary regressions, while many minimax-based methods require optimization over separate critic classes. We propose pairwise Bellman validation (PBV), a family of penalized Bellman tournament methods that reduces validation to computing held-out sample averages. PBV constructs critics from pairwise candidate differences, on the log scale for occupancy ratios, and selects the candidate with the smallest worst-case penalized score. This construction approximates oracle critics given by $Q$-function errors and log ratios of candidate to true occupancy ratios, whose Bellman and adjoint Bellman moments control estimation error. Critic penalties account for approximation error under candidate-class misspecification. We establish finite-sample oracle inequalities relative to the best available candidate, even under candidate-class misspecification. For $Q$-function selection, unweighted PBV avoids importance weighting but requires a coercivity condition on a quadratic form induced by the Bellman operator. Importance-weighted PBV (IW-PBV) uses marginalized importance weighting to exploit Bellman contraction under the target-policy occupancy measure, avoiding this condition. For occupancy-ratio selection, adjoint PBV (A-PBV) exploits KL contraction of the adjoint Bellman operator to obtain oracle guarantees under the offline data law. On Hopper and DeepOPE, unweighted PBV is competitive with LSTD-Tournament, often achieving higher accuracy on Hopper, while importance weighting can further improve performance under controlled overlap.

items.title: When Listwise Deletion Works: Causal Diagrams and Complete-Case Regression
items.summary: Listwise deletion (LWD) appears more common than imputation: at least 50% of the observational causal studies we review in leading journals state or imply it, while 7% describe an imputation model. We develop a framework for when complete-case regression consistently estimates the population average treatment effect (ATE). With a constant unit-level treatment effect, two checks suffice: whether covariates and the missingness indicator satisfy the adjustment criterion in an augmented causal diagram (DAG), and whether the estimator pools within-covariate comparisons appropriately, possibly using inverse propensity weighting. A collider--mediator illustration highlights the first check: the same missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism can require different adjustment choices. With heterogeneous effects, conditional effects must be transportable to the population and be reweighted to its population distribution. These formal results provide practical checks for applied researchers to run complete case regressions, recover existing guidance as special cases, and are illustrated with applications across fields.

items.title: Maximum score and non-smooth M-estimators with multiway dependence
items.summary: Under i.i.d. sampling, the maximum score estimator of Manski (1975) converges at the cube-root rate to a non-Gaussian limit, and under median independence alone no regular estimator attains the parametric rate Chamberlain (1986). We show that, under multiway dependence and low-level conditions, the estimator is asymptotically normal at a parametric rate in the smallest number of clusters and, when the cluster-level variance is non-degenerate, as fast as regular estimators such as probit. The result rests on a general theory for non-smooth M-estimators, under which a modified bootstrap is first-order valid given a consistent Hessian estimate. With two-way clustering a cube-root term can remain. We then develop two-scale non-standard asymptotics, in which the limit is a Gaussian vector plus an independent Chernoff-type vector and either term may dominate, along sequences of laws from a non-degenerate cluster-level variance to the degenerate case. Under high-level conditions, the symmetric bootstrap intervals for suitable scalar parameters control size uniformly over such classes of laws, asymptotically exactly where the Gaussian term dominates and conservatively otherwise.

items.title: Choice via Dual Ownership
items.summary: When there are multiple agents (or rationales), an ownership rule assigns the choice for each menu to one of them. We study choice under dual ownership, where decision control alternates between two preferences. The main contribution is the behavioral characterization of a rule that endogenously decides ownership to maximize consensus. We also axiomatize two simpler exogenous rules. Identification results are provided for each rule.

items.title: Contractual Structure and Obvious Manipulation in Many-to-Many Matching
items.summary: We study how contractual structure affects worst-case and best-case obvious manipulation in many-to-many matching with substitutable preferences. Efficient individually rational mechanisms rule out best-case obvious manipulations on both the full substitutable domain and the unitary domain. Under simple and economically natural conditions on hospitals' choices, every stable mechanism on the full domain admits obvious manipulations in both cases; hospital-proposing deferred acceptance can admit both types even under unitary doctors' preferences. A further sufficient condition makes efficient stable-dominating mechanisms obviously manipulable in the worst case. On the unitary domain, doctor-proposing deferred acceptance is not obviously manipulable. If each doctor--hospital pair has at most one feasible contract, this positive conclusion extends to every stable-dominating mechanism.

items.title: Doubly robust estimation of direct and spillover effects using multiple pre-treatment periods
items.summary: Under interference, the treatment of some units affects the outcomes of others, so that the effect on a treated unit consists of a direct and a spillover component. A non-treated comparison group then generally identifies neither component, but the difference between the total effect on the treated and the spillover effect on the comparison units. Under certain identifying assumptions, both components may be identified separately when multiple pre-treatment periods are available, even in the absence of an uncontaminated comparison group. Under a no-anticipation assumption, pre-treatment outcomes are free of both components for every unit. Extrapolating the pre-treatment trend within a group, as in interrupted time-series approaches, therefore identifies the counterfactual outcome in the absence of any treatment, provided that the model used for the extrapolation is correctly specified. Applied to the treated it gives the total effect on them, applied to the non-treated at a given level of exposure the spillover effect on them. Disentangling the two components in addition requires effect homogeneity across treated and non-treated units with the same exposure and covariates, as well as common support in exposure. We derive doubly robust and Neyman-orthogonal expressions for the effects of interest, which permits controlling for possibly high-dimensional covariates by machine learning. A simulation study confirms the root-$n$ consistent behaviour of the estimators and the reliability of the standard errors under specific regularity conditions. We apply the framework to the compulsory licensing of enemy-owned patents in the United States in 1919. Licensing raised patenting in the licensed subclasses and in technologically close ones alike, so that a comparison-group design understates the total effect.

items.title: Improving control over unobservables with network data
items.summary: This paper develops a method to conduct causal inference in the presence of unobserved confounders by leveraging networks with homophily, a frequently observed tendency to form edges with similar nodes. I introduce a concept of asymptotic homophily, according to which individuals' selectivity scales with the size of the potential connection pool. The resulting network formation model accommodates common empirical features such as homophily, degree heterogeneity, sparsity, and clustering, and provides a framework to obtain consistent estimators of treatment effects that are robust to selection on unobservables. In an application, I recover an estimate of the effect of parental involvement on students' test scores that is greater than that of OLS, arguably due to the estimator's ability to account for unobserved ability.

items.title: Unequal Rewards and the Direction of Scientific Work: Evidence from U.S. Public Universities
items.summary: Research on pay dispersion has long asked whether unequal rewards increase or depress performance. Tournament theory expects stronger effort, while social comparison accounts expect withdrawal. Both perspectives, however, treat performance as a single scale on which workers can be ranked. Scientific work often resists such ordering. Some contributions extend recognized lines of inquiry and can be evaluated against prevailing standards; others revise the frames through which value is judged and become legible only later. We argue that intellectual tournaments more readily reward the first kind of contribution than the second. Pay dispersion may therefore be associated not only with how much scholars produce but also with what kinds of intellectual exploration are encouraged. We test this argument with administrative payroll records for 105,050 tenure-line faculty in 4,839 departments at 93 U.S. public universities from 2004 to 2026, linked to publication histories in OpenAlex. For each department, we estimate a separate pay equation using rank, contract basis, and seniority, then measure the Gini of the salary variation this local ladder cannot explain. Scholars in departments with greater unexplained pay dispersion publish more papers and receive more citations, but their work is less disruptive, less novel, and more conventional. Additional analyses show that compensation premiums above the ladder go disproportionately to scholars with broad collaborations and topical breadth. Although the design cannot fully separate treatment from selection, the evidence shows that inequality is not only a distributional outcome but also an evaluative structure, shaping which forms of knowledge are recognized, rewarded, and reproduced within organizations and communities.

items.title: AI Search as an Information Intermediary: Clickstream Evidence on Web Traffic
items.summary: AI search retrieves web information to ground generated answers. We study this new information intermediary using U.S. desktop clickstream data observing use alongside referrals during ChatGPT Search's rollout. Referrals accompany 5.4% of ChatGPT sessions versus 31.1% of Google queries. Ad-supported sites receive a smaller share of ChatGPT than Google referrals, while reference and technical sites receive larger shares. Conventional searches (Google, Bing, Yahoo) decline after ChatGPT adoption, sooner when adoption follows ChatGPT Search's expansion to users without accounts. Among existing users, that expansion raises ChatGPT use; conventional searches show no detectable overall change but fall among households with lower prior search activity. These findings suggest AI search can reshape open-web traffic through its own referrals and changes in conventional search.

items.title: Price co-movement and price information diverge across Nordic electricity zones after the energy crisis
items.summary: After the 2021-2022 energy crisis, day-ahead prices in Nordic bidding zones no longer move together. We ask whether this divergence also changes the information carried by prices. The answer matters for integrating variable renewable energy (VRE), because it can help identify where wind and solar forecasts are worth producing, publishing, and using. We measured the co-movement of each Norwegian and Swedish zone with Germany-Luxembourg (DE-LU) in 2018-2025. We then used a single model, selected on 2024 data, to forecast 2025 prices at 11:00 on the previous day and tested which inputs improved accuracy in each zone. The zones moved alike until 2019, but co-movement diverged in Sweden in 2020 and in Norway in 2021, and the split has persisted. In 2024, four southern zones co-moved strongly with DE-LU (intraday correlations of 0.54-0.71), while four northern zones co-moved weakly (0.25-0.30). Yet price information did not follow this split. Previous-day neighbouring prices reduced mean absolute error by at most 2.2% in any zone, equally in coupled and isolated zones. Removing the transmission system operators' wind and solar forecasts increased mean absolute error by at most 6% in Norway, 8-16% in Sweden, and 31% in DE-LU, and the ordering held in 2024. Within Norway, the value of these forecasts showed no detectable dependence on reservoir filling. The divergence in co-movement was therefore not matched by a divergence in price information, which differed mainly between national generation systems. Thus, a zone's coupling to the continent does not indicate the value of VRE forecasts there.

items.title: Uniform Inference for Two-Way Clustered Data
items.summary: We establish uniformly asymptotically exact inference for the population mean of two-way clustered data, allowing the data-generating process to vary with sample size. This finding does not contradict the well-known impossibility result of Menzel (2021), which places a fundamental limit on uniform estimation of the asymptotic distribution of the normalized full-array mean. We estimate the same population mean by averaging the sample means from random matchings. A closed-form standard error makes the resulting confidence interval straightforward to implement. The variance estimator is positive semidefinite and the studentized matching estimator is uniformly asymptotically standard normal. The cost of uniform validity is a slower convergence rate under degeneracy. We extend the result to smooth functions of GMM parameters, allowing the different moment components to exhibit different dependence regimes. In simulations, the proposed confidence intervals achieve coverage close to the nominal level across the dependence regimes considered.

items.title: Ramping Procurement and Bid-Cost Recovery in Real-Time Market
items.summary: We study ramping procurement co-optimized with economic dispatch under net-demand uncertainty. We examine two flexible ramp product designs implemented by grid operators: single-interval and multi-interval co-optimization. Both rely on rolling-window stochastic optimization with binding and advisory interval decisions. We develop analytical frameworks to evaluate generator profits, consumer payments, bid cost recovery (BCR), and operational efficiency. In particular, net-demand uncertainty may lead to generator under-compensation, requiring discriminatory BCR. While operational efficiency is invariant to energy and ramp prices, producer profits and consumer payments depend critically on pricing. We examine locational marginal pricing (LMP) and two uniform pricing: maximum dispatch cost pricing (MDCP) and maximum temporal locational marginal pricing (MTLMP). With out-of-market BCR, LMP yields discriminatory energy prices, whereas MDCP eliminates BCR and MTLMP does so in most cases. This property enables us to establish truthful bidding incentives for price-taking generators under MDCP. Our analysis highlights trade-offs between single- and multi-interval co-optimization and pricing designs: multi-interval energy-ramp co-optimization outperforms single-interval co-optimization when ramping forecasts are accurate and ramping needs are tight, but its advantage diminishes under large forecast errors and moderate ramping needs. Empirical results on CAISO and ERCOT data show that MDCP and MTLMP increase producer profits with negligible BCR, albeit at the expense of higher consumer payments relative to LMP.

items.title: Localizing Mean Shifts in High-Dimensional Vector Autoregressive Models
items.summary: We study the localization of mean changes in high-dimensional vector autoregressions (VARs) when the autoregressive dynamics remain common across regimes.
